It starts in the middle of the action, runs thirty seconds, and has no logo, phone, app or sales voice; the brand appears only as one word in the last second. Because it is wordless, the same film works in every country with no dubbing. The feeling at the end is "I want that trip with my friends".

episodes.title: The Big Bag
episodes.story: Lola wants to hurry to the stadium, but Timo has packed a suitcase as big as a door for one night and it slows them on every stair and street. Then the rain comes, a giant umbrella pops out of the suitcase and covers everyone, and Lola hugs the bag.

episodes.title: Wake Up
episodes.story: Sunrise in the hostel on match day: Lola, dressed with her scarf on, wants to wake Timo and Yuki, but open curtains, pulled blankets and a shaken bunk bed do nothing. Then she softly claps the football clap, four arms shoot up from the bunks and clap back, and one second later both friends are out of the door before her.

episodes.title: Sleeps Anywhere
episodes.story: Yuki falls asleep sitting on Timo's giant suitcase, it rolls away down the hill, and Lola and Timo chase it through the whole town while she sleeps through every bump. It stops softly right in front of the stadium: Yuki wakes up fresh and first, and her two friends arrive and drop down beside her, laughing.

episodes.title: No Scarf
episodes.story: Lola already has her scarf, so at the scarf stand she shakes her head, crosses her arms and walks past, then past again, more slowly. Hard cut: she walks away wearing the home scarf, the hat and a flag as a cape, and the smiling seller is wearing hers.

episodes.title: One Beat Late
episodes.story: Outside the stadium everybody claps the home clap, and big Timo claps one beat late every time. A small local kid with a drum shows him, slow and then fast, and by the end Timo is the loudest of all, with the kid drumming on his shoulders.

episodes.title: Lucky Snack
episodes.story: Lola only wants to see a goal, but each time she runs out for food the stadium roars, the food jumps on her tray, and she has missed it again. So her friends push her out on purpose, the roar comes, and Lola celebrates in the sunny corridor with the food seller while her friends run out to hug their lucky charm.

pilot.title: The Big Bag
pilot.header: When your friend packs for one night (on screen from the first frame to the end of shot 3, about twelve seconds, then it leaves)
pilot.retell: Her friend brought a giant suitcase for one night and it slowed everyone down, but when it started to rain a huge umbrella popped out of it and kept them all dry on the way to the match.

shots.place: Station square of a small sunny hill town, early morning: low golden sun, long shadows, pastel houses. Far away over the roofs, four stadium floodlight masts.
shots.who: Lola and Timo
shots.seen: It starts in the middle of the action. Lola's face, close, on the left: eyes wide, mouth open. A hot-pink suitcase as tall as her shoulder and as wide as a door rolls in from the right and stops in front of her nose. Her eyes go from its wheels up to its top. Timo's happy face leans out from behind it and he waves. Lola hooks a thumb under the strap of her tiny turquoise backpack, shows it to him, and raises one eyebrow.
shots.heard: none (no words). The theme starts on the first frame: handclaps, shaker, guitar. Suitcase wheels rumbling on stone and a soft thud as it stops. Lola: a small gasp. Timo: a happy "ha!".
shots.caption: none

shots.place: A long stone staircase climbing between peach and mint houses, morning sun, washing lines overhead. The floodlight masts at the top of the hill, a little closer.
shots.who: Timo, Lola, Yuki; passing home fans out of focus
shots.seen: Timo walks backwards up the steps and pulls the suitcase up one step at a time; it lands on each step with a bump. Below it Lola pushes with both hands and one shoulder, feet slipping, cheeks blown out. Behind her Yuki climbs with her eyes closed, travel pillow round her neck, holding on to Lola's backpack. Fans in orange scarves, soft and out of focus, pass them easily, two steps at a time.
shots.heard: none. Bump, bump, bump of the suitcase, each one on a drum beat. Lola's effort breaths. One small snore from Yuki. The bass joins the theme.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: A steep cobbled street in full sun, lemon trees in pots, a low wall along one side. The masts are bigger now.
shots.who: Lola, Timo (at the front edge of the frame), an orange street cat
shots.seen: Side view. Lola pushes the suitcase uphill from behind, her whole body leaning, hardly moving; Timo pulls at the front, relaxed. On the low wall beside them a fat orange cat strolls past, overtakes them, looks back at Lola, flicks its tail and walks on. Lola watches the cat go, then lets her forehead drop against the suitcase.
shots.heard: none. Small suitcase wheels grinding slowly on cobbles. Lola: a long breath out that turns into half a laugh. The guitar riff.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: A small open square at the top of the street, still sunny; one fat cloud in the blue sky.
shots.who: Lola, close, with the side of the suitcase
shots.seen: Lola leans her back on the suitcase, out of breath. She turns her head and gives the suitcase a long sideways look, one eyebrow up. A fat raindrop lands on her nose. She goes cross-eyed at it, then slowly looks up at the sky.
shots.heard: none. The music stops dead on her look. Silence, then one "plip" on her nose and the first soft patter of rain on stone.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: The same square: heavy rain falling through bright sunshine, wet stones shining gold.
shots.who: Lola and Timo with the suitcase between them; home fans out of focus behind
shots.seen: Rain pours down. Lola holds her scarf over her head with both hands, shoulders up, eyes squeezed shut; behind them blurred fans run for cover. Next to her Timo stands calm and does not hurry: he looks up at the rain, smiles, and pats the top of the suitcase twice with his big flat hand.
shots.heard: none. Loud rain on stone. Lola: a small squeal. Then Timo's two pats, which sound exactly like the two handclaps of the theme.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: The same square, rain in sunshine.
shots.who: Lola and Timo; Yuki asleep on her feet at the edge of the frame
shots.seen: Framed like shot 1: Lola's face close on the left, the suitcase in the middle, Timo behind it. A pole shoots straight up out of the top of the suitcase and a huge umbrella with hot-pink and turquoise stripes snaps open above them, filling the top of the frame. The rain no longer hits them; pink and turquoise light falls on their faces. Lola lowers her scarf, looks up with her mouth open, looks at Timo (a small shrug and his slow smile), then throws both arms round the suitcase and presses her cheek against it, eyes closed. At the edge of the frame Yuki sleeps on, standing, dry.
shots.heard: none. A big soft "whump" as the umbrella opens. The theme comes back at full: drums, brass, the group "oh-oh-oh-oh". Rain drumming on the fabric. Lola laughing.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: The wide street to the stadium, late-morning sun shining through the rain. Straight ahead the four floodlight masts, tall and bright; a soft stream of fans with scarves moving toward them.
shots.who: Lola, Timo, Yuki, the orange cat and two home fans, all seen from behind
shots.seen: From behind: the pink suitcase rolls away from us toward the floodlights with the big striped umbrella standing on top of it. Under it Timo pushes; Lola walks with one arm round the suitcase, gives it two soft pats and leans her head on it; Yuki shuffles along with her head hanging, asleep; the orange cat sits on top of the suitcase, dry. Two fans in orange scarves squeeze in under the edges and Timo makes room. Then the umbrella shivers and pigeons burst up from the roofs: every head lifts, Yuki's arms shoot straight up into the air, and the whole group starts to run toward the lights, the umbrella bouncing.
shots.heard: none. The stadium roar rolling down the street, muffled and huge. Yuki: one loud happy shout with no words. Everyone laughing, wheels rattling fast. The group "oh-oh-oh-oh" and the last two handclaps as the picture cuts back to the start.
shots.caption: none

pilot.end_card: The word VENUVOY in white, centred, over the last second of shot 7 (the umbrella rolling toward the floodlights), with one small line under it: "See you at the next match." Nothing else: no logo animation, no app, no link.

risks: The handmade puppet look could read as children's television. Guard: adult proportions, streetwear, close handheld camera, real-sun light and the dance track; make one still and one 5-second test clip first and show them to two or three people aged 18 to 25. Plan B: keep the same wordless scripts and move to a less cute finish (smooth stylised 3D with real-fabric textures); nothing has to be rewritten because nobody speaks.

Faces, outfits or style drifting between clips. Guard: one reference sheet per friend (front, side, back, six expressions), one locked outfit and one owned colour each, every clip started from an approved still, any clip with a changed outfit rejected. Plan B: two people per frame; Yuki can be taken out of shots 2 and 6 and the cat out of shots 3 and 7 without changing the story.

The suitcase changing size or colour from shot to shot. Guard: a prop sheet with a fixed scale (top level with Lola's shoulder, turquoise strap) and a person always beside it. Plan B: frame it cropped so only part of it is seen.

The umbrella rising out of the suitcase is an object changing shape, which generated video does badly. Guard: never animate the mechanism; hard cut from Timo's two pats to a still in which the umbrella is already almost open, and let the "whump" and the brass sell it. Plan B: start shot 6 with it fully open and bouncing.

Rain may turn the picture grey, start badly, or the single drop on the nose may not appear. Guard: sunlit rain on a warm grade, the downpour present from the first frame of shot 5, the single drop and extra streaks added in the edit. Plan B: change the weather to fierce midday sun: Lola hides under her scarf from the heat and the umbrella gives shade; same shots, same story.
Three or more figures and passing fans in shots 2 and 7. Guard: passers-by soft, from behind, no faces; shot 7 is filmed from behind so no face has to match. Plan B: the trio only.

The story not landing without sound. Guard: before publishing, show the silent cut to a fresh viewer and to the AI test viewer and ask "what happened?"; publish only if the answer matches the retell sentence. Plan B: hold the unclear shot longer, or replace shot 3 with a second stairs beat; the top line stays as the safety net.

The first series' slips returning (a black band, a prop that jumps, voices that change). Guard: every still composed in 9:16 with the top 15 percent free, every clip checked for bars before the edit, props never change hands (suitcase with Timo, backpack on Lola), and there are no spoken voices to drift because all gasps, laughs and cheers are added in the sound mix.

Later films with clapping (Wake Up, One Beat Late): generated hands will not hit the beat on their own. Guard: cut each clap on the beat in the edit and take the clap sound from the track, not from the clip. Plan B: show the clap as two or three very short cuts of hands and faces.
The title 'Trip Trip Hooray' may already be used by a travel business. Guard: check before launch. Plan B title: 'Go Go Goal'. Every post carries the platform's AI label.

title: Plan, No Plan
premise: Two best friends travel to football matches abroad: Timo plans every minute, Luna plans nothing, and every film is one small clash between his way and her way that ends with both of them laughing.
look:
STYLISED, not photoreal: a warm handmade stop-motion look made in 3D, as if two clay figures were filmed on a miniature street in real sunlight.

CHARACTERS: matte clay skin with soft thumb marks, big readable eyes and eyebrows, simple chunky hands, sculpted hair. Clothes of felt, knit and denim at toy scale with a visible weave. Adult proportions (long legs, head about one fifth of the height) and real streetwear, so they read as 22-year-olds and not as children's TV.

WORLD: an invented sunny football town built like a model. Painted houses in cream, terracotta, mint and sky blue, cobbled streets, plain bunting, shop signs as colour blocks with no letters. The stadium is only ever a soft cream bowl with four floodlights in the distance, plus its sound.

PALETTE: cream base. Teal belongs to Timo, coral belongs to Luna, sunflower yellow is the accent they share (his watch, her suitcase). The team scarf is cream with wide teal and coral stripes: their two colours on one scarf. No black and no grey; shadows are warm.

LIGHT: always sun. Golden late afternoon is the standard, pink-gold for mornings, a sun-shower if it rains. Never night, never a dim room.

LENS: filmed as if a friend holds the camera on a miniature set. Eye level, close to faces, a small wobble, quick pans to the reaction, shallow macro focus so backgrounds melt into soft colour, light film grain, movement a little snappy like stop-motion. Vertical frames are built on the contrast of the tall thin friend and the short friend with the wide suitcase.

WARDROBE: one locked outfit per character in every film.

WHY: (1) It is honest: it does not pretend generated people are real, which this age group dislikes. (2) A buddy comedy needs cartoon physics: riding a suitcase down a hill is charming in clay and a dangerous stunt in live action. (3) It hides the weak spots of generated video: simple hands, blurred backgrounds, no text, and characters that stay the same because they are strong shapes in fixed colours. (4) Colour coding lets a twelve-year-old follow who is who with the sound off. (5) It is the opposite of the first series in every way: sun, colour and handmade warmth against grey, night and photoreal.
music:
One theme made for the series: sunny afro-house with an amapiano bounce, 122 beats per minute, major key, instrumental apart from one group hook.

Two motifs, one for each friend. Timo is a tidy tick-tock pattern on muted marimba, exactly on the beat like a watch. Luna is a loose log-drum bass with a sliding brass stab and a cowbell that lands a little late. In the verse they answer each other; in the chorus they lock together under a football-stand clap pattern (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap) and a five-note 'oh-oh-oh' sung by a handful of friends, not a big choir.

Shape for a 30-second film: tick-tock and claps for the set-up, the log drum comes in with the obstacle, one bar almost silent on the moment of doubt, then the full chorus on the payoff and the last clap-clap-clap on the end card.

Feeling: walking to the ground with your friends on a warm evening. No whistling, no ukulele, no trailer drums, no whoosh effects. Natural sound is mixed loud: suitcase wheels on stone, a far roar, a laugh that is not cut clean.

cast.name: Timo
cast.look: Tall and thin, the tallest thing in the frame; Luna reaches his shoulder. Long legs and arms, narrow shoulders, stands very straight with his chin a little forward. Dark brown skin. Long oval face, high cheekbones, big round dark-brown eyes, thick straight eyebrows that tilt up in the middle when he worries, wide mouth with a shy smile, clean-shaven. Black tight curls in a short neat flat-top fade with sharp edges. Round thin gold-wire glasses. ALWAYS: a deep teal zip-up track jacket closed to the chin with one cream stripe down each sleeve; straight dark navy trousers that end above the ankle; cream socks; clean white sneakers; a small square teal backpack worn high on both shoulders with the straps pulled tight; a sunflower-yellow plastic watch on his LEFT wrist. Team scarf (cream with wide teal and coral stripes, cream fringe) knotted once at the throat, both ends exactly the same length. No words, no badge anywhere. His colour is teal.
cast.personality: Has planned every minute and loves being early. Carries a spare of everything in a tiny backpack. Moves in straight lines, quick and exact: taps his watch, pushes his glasses up with one finger, counts on his fingers. When the plan breaks he freezes for one beat with his eyebrows up, then gives in and enjoys it more than anyone. Gentle, never bossy, the first to laugh at himself. Voice (locked): soft, quick, clear light tenor, neutral international English.

cast.name: Luna
cast.look: Short and sturdy with strong legs; comes up to Timo's shoulder; stands with her weight on one hip and is never quite still. East Asian features, warm light-tan skin, round face with full cheeks, a few freckles across the nose, dark eyes that close into crescents when she laughs, short straight eyebrows, a wide grin with a small gap between the front teeth. Black blunt bob to the chin, always messy, short fringe, ONE coral-pink streak at the front left. ALWAYS: an oversized coral retro football shirt with a cream collar and cream cuffs, completely plain (no badge, number or words), half tucked in on one side; baggy light-blue denim shorts to the knee; odd socks pulled up, one sunflower yellow and one cream; chunky cream sneakers, scuffed, laces loose. The same team scarf worn loose and lopsided: one end short, the other hanging to her knee. On travel days: a sunflower-yellow hard suitcase as tall as her chest, a plain rounded box with two raised ridges and four black wheels, no stickers. Her colour is coral.
cast.personality: Says yes to everything, plans nothing, and somehow it works. Always hungry, always a little late, never worried; sleeps anywhere and makes a friend in ten seconds. Moves in curves: drifts towards food, music and dogs. Big laugh with her head thrown back. Teases Timo and then hugs him. Half of whatever she is eating belongs to whoever stands next to her. Knows she would miss every train without him. Voice (locked): low, a little husky, loud, laughs in the middle of words, neutral international English.

why_clear:
1. Two people, two colours, two props. The tall teal one with the watch and tiny backpack is the plan; the short coral one with the giant yellow suitcase is no plan. Nobody needs a name or a word to know who is who.
2. Every film has the same simple shape: his way, her way, the clash, the two ways together, both laughing. Once you have seen one, you can read all of them.
3. The want is visible in the first shot (a watch being tapped, a stadium far away, a sandwich box, a sleeping friend) and the obstacle is a physical thing in the frame, never an idea.
4. The story is carried by coarse actions and faces: dragging, pointing, shaking the head, sitting, riding, hugging. The spoken lines only say what the picture already shows; cover them and nothing is lost.
5. Nothing must be read inside the picture: no signs, screens, chats or documents. On-screen text is only the short spoken line as a caption (at most six or seven everyday words, on screen for the whole shot) and one plain 'When...' line at the top during the first two shots.
6. The last shot repeats the first with the feeling turned round (he stares at the suitcase in shock; he hugs the suitcase), so the change is seen, not explained.
7. No irony, no subtext, no joke that needs another film.
why_young_cool: Two friends of 22 and 23 you would want on your own trip, in sun and colour, with a theme built on stand claps that belongs on a playlist. The humour is situation and reaction face, the kind of teasing that ends in a hug; each of them is right in turn (her suitcase saves one film, his tiny backpack saves another), so nobody is the fool. Everyone has a Timo and a Luna in their group, which is the reason to tag a friend: 'which one are you, Plan or No Plan?'. The bold, loud, always-hungry fan is the woman; the careful one is the man. The handmade clay look feels designed and fresh instead of a glossy advert or fake real people, the camera feels like a friend filming, films run under 30 seconds and loop, and the brand says nothing until the last second.

episodes.title: One Night
episodes.story: Timo wants to reach the match on time, but Luna's giant suitcase for one night slows them on every step. At the top of the last hill she sits on it, he gets on, and they ride it down to the stadium, where he hugs the suitcase.

episodes.title: Try It
episodes.story: Timo wants to eat the neat sandwiches he brought from home; Luna keeps holding a huge steaming street-food flatbread under his nose and he keeps shaking his head. He takes one small bite, his eyes go wide, and the film ends with him holding one in each hand while she happily eats his sandwiches.

episodes.title: Left or Right
episodes.story: Both want to get to the stadium; at a fork Timo points left along his planned route, Luna points right towards the drums, and each goes their own way. He marches alone down empty straight streets, she dances along behind a street drummer and a dog, and they bump into each other at the gate in the same second and walk in arm in arm.

episodes.title: Wake Up, Luna
episodes.story: At sunrise Timo is dressed with his scarf on and wants to catch the early train, but nothing wakes Luna. He holds a warm pastry in front of her nose and she follows it with her eyes shut, wrapped in her blanket, all the way to the train, where she is wide awake and he falls asleep on her shoulder.

episodes.title: Just In Case
episodes.story: On a blue-sky match day Luna laughs and points at the sun when Timo packs two rain ponchos into his tiny backpack. On the walk to the stadium a sudden sun-shower soaks her in seconds, and the film ends with both of them in ponchos, dancing through the rain while she hugs his backpack.

episodes.title: The Chant
episodes.story: In the stand everyone claps a rhythm: Timo knows it perfectly but claps tiny and shy, Luna does not know it and claps loud and wrong. An old local fan between them shows them with big slow arms, and the three end up clapping over their heads, perfectly together.

pilot.title: One Night
pilot.header: When your friend packs for one night
pilot.retell: She brought a giant suitcase for one night and it made them late for the match, so they rode it down the hill to the stadium and got there on time.

shots.place: Sunny square outside a small train station in an invented football town, late afternoon, low golden sun, long shadows, plain bunting overhead
shots.who: Timo and Luna
shots.seen: From the first frame: Timo stands close to the camera on the right, tiny teal backpack on both shoulders, tapping his yellow watch. On the left Luna walks towards him, pulling with both hands a yellow suitcase as tall as her chest, grinning. Timo's finger stops on the watch. His mouth opens. His eyes travel from the wheels up to the top of the suitcase. She parks it between them with a bump and it wobbles.
shots.heard: Timo: "Luna. It is one night!" Natural sound: suitcase wheels rattling on stone with one squeak, the bump, drums far away. Music: tick-tock marimba and claps.
shots.caption: Luna. It is one night!

shots.place: Same square, same light
shots.who: Luna with the suitcase; Timo's shoulder at the edge of the frame
shots.seen: Close on Luna. She leans one elbow on top of the suitcase, pats its side twice with her free hand the way you pat a horse, and smiles with all her teeth.
shots.heard: Luna: "I know! This is the small one!" Natural sound: two hollow pats on the suitcase.
shots.caption: This is the small one!

shots.place: Wide stone steps going up between coloured houses, same golden light
shots.who: Timo at the top, near the camera; Luna below on the steps
shots.seen: Luna walks backwards up the steps, leaning back, pulling the suitcase up with both hands. It bumps up one step, then one more, slowly. She puffs her cheeks out, still smiling. At the top Timo taps his watch, looks at her, looks at the watch again and bounces on his toes.
shots.heard: none. Natural sound: bump... bump... of the suitcase on stone, Luna puffing, Timo's shoes tapping fast, the far roar a little louder. Music: the log drum comes in.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: Top of a long straight street that runs gently downhill; at the very bottom the stadium, small, bright and out of focus, floodlights shining in the sun
shots.who: Timo and Luna, seen from just behind their shoulders, the suitcase between them
shots.seen: The street drops away in front of them, empty, all the way down to the small bright stadium. Timo points at the stadium with a straight arm, turns his face to Luna (we see it from the side), taps his watch three times fast and puts both hands on his head. Luna, out of breath, one hand on the suitcase, looks down the slope, then down at the suitcase wheels, then down the slope again. One corner of her mouth goes up.
shots.heard: Timo: "The match starts in five minutes!" Natural sound: crowd roar and drums rising from far below.
shots.caption: The match starts in five minutes!

shots.place: Same hilltop, camera now low in front of them, the slope behind the camera
shots.who: Luna and Timo
shots.seen: Luna is already sitting on top of the suitcase, facing down the hill, feet off the ground, grinning. She pats the empty space behind her twice and lifts her eyebrows at Timo. Timo, standing beside the suitcase, shakes his head, shows both palms and takes one step back.
shots.heard: Timo: "No. No, no, no." Natural sound: Luna's giggle, one squeak of a wheel. Music: drops to the tick-tock alone for one bar.
shots.caption: No. No, no, no.

shots.place: The downhill street, empty, sun flashing between the houses, bunting rushing past overhead
shots.who: Luna and Timo, both sitting on the suitcase
shots.seen: Hard cut. They ride the suitcase down the street straight towards the camera, which races backwards just in front of them. Luna sits in front with both arms in the air and her mouth wide open in a laugh, hair and scarf flying back. Timo sits behind her with his arms wrapped round her shoulders, eyes huge, mouth open in a scream, glasses crooked. After two seconds his scream turns into a laugh and he lifts one fist in the air. The houses streak past on both sides.
shots.heard: none. Natural sound: wheels roaring on stone, wind, Timo's long scream turning into laughter, Luna's "Wooo!", the crowd roar growing. Music: the full chorus hits, claps and the group 'oh-oh-oh'.
shots.caption: none

shots.place: Open space in front of the stadium: the entrance is a bright soft blur behind them, two or three out-of-focus fans in the same scarves far back, low golden sun
shots.who: Timo and Luna
shots.seen: The suitcase stands still. Timo is on his knees next to it, out of breath, glasses crooked. He looks at his watch and breaks into a huge smile. Then he wraps both arms round the yellow suitcase and presses his cheek against it with his eyes shut. Behind him Luna is bent over with her hands on her knees, laughing; she drops one arm round his shoulders.
shots.heard: Timo: "I love this suitcase." Natural sound: Luna's big laugh, the stadium roar swelling as the match begins. Music: chorus to the final clap-clap-clap.
shots.caption: I love this suitcase.

pilot.end_card: Last 2 seconds, over the softly blurred final frame (total film about 29 seconds): the word VENUVOY, and under it in small letters: See you at the next match. Heard: the final clap-clap-clap of the theme and one 'oh-oh'. Nothing else. The last picture (the yellow suitcase) loops into the first.

risks: The ride (shot 6) is the hardest clip: the suitcase may change shape, the wheels may look wrong or the two may slide off. Plan: start from a still with both already seated and ask only for rolling forward, hair and scarves blown back and the street streaming past, 4 to 5 seconds. Plan B: replace it with two easy clips cut fast: a close-up of their two faces in the wind with the background streaking (wheels out of frame) and a low shot of the wheels rattling over the cobbles. Plan C: Timo runs downhill pulling the suitcase with Luna sitting on it, arms up. The story holds in all three.

Style drift: the clay look can slide into glossy plastic 3D or half-photoreal between shots. Plan: design and approve all seven start stills in one look before any video is made, with one fixed style paragraph and the same reference pictures for every shot. Plan B: accept a simpler clean matte 3D look with the same palette and light, but never mix two looks in one film.

The look could read as children's TV instead of young and cool. Plan: adult proportions, streetwear, natural adult voices, the handheld camera and the dance theme; show the character sheet to three people aged 18 to 25 before anything else is generated. Plan B: move one step towards a designer-toy or painterly 3D look and keep the palette, cast and scripts unchanged.

Character details drifting (glasses, watch on the left wrist, the pink streak, odd socks, scarf stripes). Plan: one locked outfit, a character sheet with front, side, back and five expressions, and a checklist run on every start still. Plan B: frame tighter (chest up) so fewer details must match, and reduce the scarf to two wide stripes.

The suitcase changing size between shots. Plan: one rule in every still: its top is level with Luna's chest; it is a plain yellow rounded box with two ridges and four black wheels, no logo or stickers. Plan B: let the frame crop part of it so exact size cannot be compared.

Voices changing between shots or films, and weak lip-sync (the first series had both). Plan: one speaker per shot, lines of four to seven words, the speaker's face large; lock one voice per character from the first approved take and run every later line through the same two voices. Plan B: the film is written to work silent, so a shot whose line fails is used without speech and without its caption, with music and natural sound only. The final hug needs no line.
The steps (shot 3): the suitcase may melt into the steps or climb by itself. Plan B: a cobbled uphill street instead of steps; dragging a suitcase on a slope is reliable.

Garbled text or a crowd in focus at the stadium (shots 4 and 7) and on shop fronts. Plan: the stadium is always small or blurred, background fans are two or three soft shapes, signs are blank colour blocks, no shirt has letters. Plan B: stage shot 7 against a sunlit wall with floodlight shadows and bunting, and let the roar tell us where they are.

Too much action in one clip (shots 1, 4 and 7 each hold two or three beats). Plan: every start still begins as late as possible (Luna already arriving, Timo already on his knees), and each clip asks for at most three simple actions. Plan B: let one generated clip carry only the first beat and cut early; shots 1 and 2 can also be made from one clip with a jump cut.

Framing slips such as a black band at the top or a face under the header line. Plan: generate every clip at full 9:16, keep the top eighth of each still free of faces for the header, and check the top and bottom edges of every clip before the edit.

Riding a suitcase down a street could be read as a stunt to copy. Plan: the clay world, an empty street with no cars, a gentle slope and a soft stop keep it clearly cartoon. Plan B is plan C of the ride: Timo pulls, Luna sits.

Posting: the films must carry the platform's AI label; the designed look makes that label feel natural instead of a confession. No hand-to-hand passing of objects, no phone, no ticket and no screen appear anywhere in the pilot, so the slips of the first series cannot repeat.

scores.best: The only one with real jokes and real friends. 'Kofi. It is one night.' / 'You never know.' / 'Do you have ketchup?' / 'Next time, bring two.' are lines I would quote in a group chat, and the ketchup beat is a second laugh that comes from character, not from the plot. It also has no header line at all, so it never looks like a brand meme page. 'No Voice' (nobody can speak the morning after, and the waiter croaks back because he was there too) is the best episode idea in the whole pack: true, funny and warm with no effort.
scores.worst: Maya is the one who is wrong in four of the six films, so she slides into the nagging mum-friend and the girl gets taught a lesson every week. The town is populated only by 'round, friendly older people', and with 'food and laughter instead of beer and shouting' and a 'happy, a little lazy' 118 BPM the whole thing can tip into a sweet children's short. The pilot has no physical high point (ponchos are true but dorky), and nobody in a football series wears a football shirt.
scores.steal: The look reference itself: collectible art-toy figures in streetwear with adult proportions, not 'clay puppets'. That one phrase decides whether the series looks like something a 23-year-old collects or something a five-year-old watches.

scores.best: The best single moment and the best title. 'No. No, no, no.' then a hard cut to both of them flying downhill on the suitcase, his scream turning into a laugh, is the clip I would actually send. 'I know! This is the small one!' is the funniest line in any pilot. Luna (messy bob with a coral streak, half-tucked retro football shirt, odd socks, laughs in the middle of words) is the coolest and best-dressed character on the table, and 'Plan or No Plan, which one are you?' is a share hook that needs no begging.
scores.worst: A boy and a girl alone on trips reads as a couple, not as a friend group, so the feeling is rom-com instead of 'me and my friends'. The odd-couple formula (his way, her way, clash, laugh) is a sitcom format a grown-up would pitch, and by film four I know the ending before it starts. 'The match starts in five minutes!' is a line written for the plot, not something a person says. The 'When your friend...' header is brand-account meme language.
scores.steal: The refusal followed by a hard cut to the opposite ('No. No, no, no.' then the ride, scream turning into laughter). Every film should have one cut like that: it is the native joke rhythm of the feed and the frame people screenshot.

scores.best: The front camera puts me inside the group: faces close, friends squeezing into frame, the camera handed to a friend. The closing picture of three laughing faces jammed into one selfie is the warmest thumbnail in the pack, and 'The Train Home' (she films her sleeping friends, then gets filmed asleep with her mouth open) is exactly what friends do to each other. It starts mid-action with no 'hey guys', which is right.
scores.worst: An animated character talking to the lens is still a fake vlogger, just a cute one: it is a brand inventing an influencer, and after two years of AI selfie-vlog clips the format now smells of AI slop and of arriving late to a trend. Nina performing for the camera in every single shot ('Okay. I love this suitcase', taking a bow) is try-hard, the other two become her props, and one camera angle for six films gets samey. The header 'One night away. Otto brought a giant suitcase.' explains the joke before it happens.
scores.steal: End every film on one front-camera frame: three faces squeezed in, laughing, filmed by one of them. Use the selfie as the signature last shot, not as the whole format.

scores.best: The most energy in the first second (a sprinting face shouting 'Otto! Run! The train!') and the best season ending: the top of the stairs, the light and the roar open, the pitch shines below and sleepy Sami's eyes are wide open for the first time. Every fan knows that moment. Sami hugging a worn football as a pillow and waking for exactly one line ('Are we there?') is lovable, and 'First Away' is real fan language.
scores.worst: 'Mission 1: catch the train' sitting on screen for the whole film is a learning app for children; 'the language of games' is an adult's idea of what young people like, and the number makes it look like homework I missed. The mood is earnest and sweet rather than cool: a kind local rescues them in almost every film, and the old man giving away his scarf is a Christmas-advert beat. Clay at 12 frames a second with slightly big heads pushes it further toward kids' television.
scores.steal: The season's last image: the climb to the top row, then the pitch opening below as light, green and roar, with the calmest friend finally wide awake. Keep it as the finale of whatever series wins.

scores.best: The fat orange cat that strolls past on the wall, overtakes them, looks back and flicks its tail is a real laugh with no words, and the craft is sharp: the music stops dead on Lola's look, Timo's two pats land as the two claps of the theme, and the film loops. Yuki with the sleep mask and travel pillow, asleep standing in the rain, is a great silhouette.
scores.worst: Wordless clay puppets doing slapstick is children's television or an in-flight safety film, however long the legs are. With no voices there is no teasing, nothing to quote and nobody I feel I know, and friends who never talk are mascots, not people I want to travel with. An umbrella shooting out of a suitcase is cartoon magic, not something that happens on a trip. 'Trip Trip Hooray' is a dad pun and the most cringe title here, and 'When your friend...' is an old meme format.
scores.steal: The orange street cat as a running local who quietly judges them (it overtakes the suitcase, looks back, walks on). The feed loves a cat, and it is a second punchline that costs no dialogue.

advice:
Away Crew wins for me because it has the only script that sounds like friends, but as written I would make it, not fight for it. To get there:

1. Kill the kids'-TV risk before anything else. Art toy, not nursery: longer legs, eyes smaller than feels safe, scuffed trainers, a half-tucked shirt, odd socks. Put one plain retro football shirt on someone, because right now nobody in a football series wears one and vintage shirts are what this age group actually wears. Show the three-friend line-up still to real 18 to 25 year olds and ask only "who is this made for?". If anyone says "kids", fix the still, not the video.

2. Watch the music. Claps plus a bright guitar plus a group "oh-oh" is one step from stomp-clap advert music, which my age group openly mocks. Lead with the log drum and shaker, make it knock on a phone speaker, and keep the voices few, rough and slightly out of tune like three mates in a stand. Use the hook only on the payoff. "A little lazy" is fine for the walk, not for the drop.

3. Give every film one moment worth a screenshot. The pilot is warm but flat. Borrow the duo's hard cut (a refusal, then the opposite) and let the laugh run uncut. The ketchup beat is the real punchline, so protect it.

4. Rotate who is wrong. Maya loses in four of six films and becomes the nag. Let her plan save them at least once, and let Kofi or Yuki cause a problem. The teasing needs a little bite; all-sweet reads as a children's show.

5. Voices decide the age. Natural, low-key, lightly accented second-language English, never perky cartoon acting. Mumbles and overlapping laughter are good.

6. Put people their own age in the town. Only round grandparents is twee. Making a friend your age at an away match is the dream, so let a young local teach the chant.

7. Do not sanitise football. Let them be properly loud and a bit feral at a goal; "No Voice" proves they were. Fans will smell a cleaned-up version.

8. Keep it un-branded in feel. No header line (keep it that way), captions in a plain native style with no coloured highlight words, an end card of about 1.5 seconds, and never write "tag your Kofi" in the post. If the characters are right, the comments do it.

9. Signature ending: finish each film on one front-camera frame of three faces squeezed in, and keep the orange cat as a recurring local.

scores.best: Nothing has to be read or heard. The whole chain is physical and in order: tiny backpack beside a door-sized suitcase, stairs, a cat overtaking them, rain, an umbrella out of the suitcase, a hug. The rescue is one huge, unmistakable object filling the top of the frame, the rain gets two shots (8 seconds) instead of one, and the payoff is an action framed as the mirror of shot 1. Retold from the 'seen' fields alone it matches the intended sentence exactly.
scores.worst: The frames are overloaded for a small phone. Shot 1 holds six beats in 4 seconds. A sleepwalking third friend who is never explained, a cat, passing fans, two strangers under the umbrella and pigeons all compete with the story. Shot 7 ends from behind with no faces, and its last beat (umbrella shivers, pigeons fly, everyone runs) is picture-code for a roar that the viewer must infer. If the umbrella is hard-cut to already open, where it came from also becomes an inference. 'One night' exists only in the header.
scores.steal: Rule 4: every sound that matters is doubled by something visibly moving. Pair it with the publish gate: show the silent cut to a fresh viewer and release only if their retelling matches the intended sentence.

scores.best: The cleanest cause and effect of the five: the same suitcase is slow uphill and fast downhill, which a child understands physically. There are only two people, told apart by height and colour. The want is a prop: the watch (tap = hurry, hands on head = late, glance plus smile = made it). The refusal, the ride and the hug are each one coarse action, and the seen fields alone retell the story.
scores.worst: Text piles up exactly while the viewer is orienting: the header and a caption are on screen together in shots 1 and 2, and five of seven shots carry a line. Two lines are verbal jokes ('This is the small one!', 'five minutes') that are lost without reading. The idea moment in shot 4 is played from behind the shoulders, with small eye movements towards small wheels. The arrival at the stadium is a soft blur, and its plan B leans on the roar, which is sound only.
scores.steal: The watch as a visible clock: one prop that shows the want, the pressure and the success with no word or number.

scores.best: One big orange object whose meaning flips carries the story. There is no header and never two texts on screen at once. Frame 1 (shock beside the suitcase) and frame 7 (hugging the suitcase) answer each other. Each shot is mostly one action plus one reaction face, and the rule that nothing is passed hand to hand removes a whole class of confusing slips.
scores.worst: The turn is crammed and partly indirect. Shot 4 squeezes the raindrop, three look-ups, the downpour, the backpack over the head, the fries and Kofi's smile into 3 seconds. The rescue is a row of folded yellow shapes that only become raincoats one cut later, and nobody is seen putting one on. The ketchup gag then leaves Maya, whose change of mind is the story, out of the frame for 4 seconds. Her want (get to the match fast) is never visible: there is no clock and no destination until shot 4, and 'one night' lives only in the caption. Five of seven shots have a line to read.
scores.steal: The caption discipline: the only text on screen is the current spoken line of 3 to 5 words, held for the whole shot, never beside a second text and with no header.

scores.best: Every film has a goal you can point at, and a train about to leave is a deadline understood everywhere. Shot 5 (the sleeping friend riding the suitcase while two friends push at a sprint) is a single picture that carries the whole solution.
scores.worst: The heaviest reading and tracking load of the five. A header stays up for the whole film while five captions come and go, so two texts compete throughout, and 'Mission 1' suggests other films are needed. There are four characters and two places cross-cut. The train is not in frame 1, only in the caption, and the urgency rests on a guard glancing at her wrist. The fix is not physically logical: a suitcase too heavy to pull becomes fast with a person sitting on it. Boarding is a blur whose plan B is sound only, and the closing beat is a verbal joke ('Are we there?').
scores.steal: Lay all seven start stills side by side like a comic strip before any video is made, and approve only if the strip alone tells the story.

scores.best: The reversal is big and physical: she laughs at the suitcase, then rides on it. The same two pats recur (Otto twice, then Nina) as a wordless refrain, and the one raised finger doubles the word 'one' with a gesture.
scores.worst: The selfie format puts a talking face in front of the story. The suitcase and the struggle on the stairs (shot 3) are small in the background of a wide lens. Three camera modes (selfie, flip, handed over) make the viewer work out who is filming. With the sound off, a face speaking into the lens signals that you are missing something. The turn has no visible cause: she is bouncing in shot 3 and collapsed in shot 4, which the concept's own risk list admits. The header is two sentences with a name. In the last shot the suitcase is barely in frame, so the payoff rests on the caption.
scores.steal: The repeated gesture as a callback: the same two pats on the lid by the owner, then by the doubter, say 'you were right' without a word.

advice:
The client's first complaint was "I understood nothing", so the winner has to pass one test before anything else: a fresh viewer watches once, muted, on a phone, and retells the film in one sentence.

These rules apply to whichever concept wins:

1. **One idea per shot, held at least 3 seconds.** Split or lengthen any shot whose "seen" field has more than two beats. That means shot 1 and shot 7 of "silent", shot 4 of "crew" and shot 4 of "duo".
2. **Only the story on screen.** In a pilot, every extra figure is a question the viewer cannot answer. For "silent", either give sleeping Yuki one clear beat of her own or take her out of shots 2 and 6. Keep the cat to shot 3 only, and drop the two strangers under the umbrella.
3. **Show the rescue come out of the suitcase.** Never cut to an umbrella that is already open with no link. Keep the pole visibly planted in the suitcase top, start with it half open, and hold the open umbrella about 1.5 seconds before the reaction. If ponchos are used instead, show one being shaken open or pulled over a head.
4. **Make the rain big.** A single drop on a nose and a sun-shower in a bright world can vanish on a small screen. Use chunky streaks, splashes on the suitcase lid, wet hair and a darker scarf.
5. **End on a face and an action, not a code.** The story finishes on the hug. Keep shot 7 of "silent" as a short walk towards the floodlights. Either drop the pigeons-and-roar beat or turn the group so we see their faces light up; nobody should have to decode why they start running.
6. **Make the want visible in frame 1.** Borrow the watch from "duo", or have the hurried friend point at the floodlight masts, so "we want to get there" is seen.
7. **One text at a time, and none that matters.** Use at most one header of 7 words or fewer in a free top band, never together with a caption. If lines are spoken, keep them to 3 to 5 words that only name what is in the picture, with no joke that lives only in a line. Test the cut with all text covered.
8. **Two gates before spending.** First, the seven start stills laid out as a strip must tell the story alone. Second, the muted cut goes to a real young viewer and a second-language adult, not only the AI viewer; release only if their sentence matches.
9. **Check the later films for sound dependence now.** "One Beat Late", "Wake Up" and "Lucky Snack" (and the chant films in the other concepts) hinge on a clap or a roar. Each needs a picture double: one pair of hands visibly out of step in a row of hands, or friends leaping and hugging seen through the doorway behind the one who missed the goal. If no picture double can be found, replace that film.

scores.best: The pilot is the one I can retell without thinking: giant suitcase annoys her, it rains, the suitcase has raincoats for everyone, she hugs it. It also asks for the least reading of all five: no header, only 3 to 5 word lines that repeat what I already see, which is the direct answer to 'I understood nothing'. Three friends give me the 'nice' feeling I asked for, and the pink-and-yellow crew scarf is something my community could actually own. The look is pitched as art-toy figures in streetwear, the coolest version of the shared look, and it is the only concept that promises me a line-up still to approve before any video is made.
scores.worst: It is the gentlest of the five: 'a little lazy' is pleasant, but the pilot has no moment that makes a friend grab my phone, like the downhill ride in the duo. It has no sharp hook either; 'three friends, one small problem' is a description, not a format people repeat. Maya is the one who is wrong in three of six films, which drifts toward making her the fool. Three people in most frames plus rain is where the screw-ups came from last time.
scores.steal: The crew scarf in colours that belong to no club: worn three ways, tied to the suitcase, lying under VENUVOY on the end card. It is the one thing in any concept that can leave the screen and become the community's badge.

scores.best: The title is the whole idea in three words that I understand as a Hebrew speaker, and 'which one are you, Plan or No Plan?' is the strongest reason to tag a friend in the whole set. Two people per frame is the safest way to keep the 'no screw-ups' promise. It has the funniest line ('This is the small one!') and the most exciting picture (riding the suitcase down the hill to the stadium). 'Plan' also quietly echoes what my product does without advertising it.
scores.worst: Two is not a crew. A tall guy and a short girl will be read as a couple by half the audience, and 'I want that trip with my friends' is weaker with a pair. The same clash shape every time can tire by film four. Timo, glasses and jacket zipped to the chin, risks being the uncool one people laugh at. The header plus captions of up to seven words is more reading than I want, and the ride is the hardest clip to generate.
scores.steal: The binary identity question as the share mechanic ('which one are you?'), together with the rule that each friend is right in turn: her suitcase saves one film, his tiny backpack with the ponchos saves another.

scores.best: Nothing to translate and nothing to mis-hear: my friends in Tel Aviv and a fan in Jakarta get the same film, and the voice and lip problems of the first series cannot happen at all. The 'When your friend packs for one night' line is how this audience already talks in the feed. 'Lucky Snack', the friend who always misses the goal, is the truest football idea in any concept.
scores.worst: Mute puppets are cute, not cool. I fear my friends say 'sweet, is it for kids?' and that nobody becomes a fan of characters with no voice and no line to quote. The umbrella shooting out of the suitcase is cartoon magic, not a trip I recognise. The last shot stacks a cat, two strangers, pigeons, a roar and a run, which is where I would get lost again. The title 'Trip Trip Hooray' sounds like a children's programme.
scores.steal: The silent-retell gate before publishing: show the cut with the sound off to someone who has seen nothing, ask 'what happened?', and publish only if the answer matches the one-sentence retelling.

scores.best: It has the two moments that would give a real fan goosebumps: the old local taking off his own faded scarf for her, and the last stair where the pitch opens and the sleepy friend's eyes are wide open for the first time. A goal named on screen ('catch the train') means I know what I am watching in the first second, and the one-day arc from sunrise to kick-off feels like a real first trip.
scores.worst: The pilot has a logic hole a twelve-year-old will spot: the suitcase is 'too heavy', so they put a person on top of it and it goes faster. That is exactly how I end up saying 'I did not understand' again. 'Mission 1' tells a new viewer they missed something, the mistake of the first series. The season ends at kick-off after six films, so there is no match and no trip home. The pilot is the riskiest to make (train doors, a fourth character, a sprint), and it carries a permanent header plus captions.
scores.steal: One film with a lump in the throat instead of a gag: the first sight of the pitch at the top of the stairs, or the old fan giving away his scarf. The series needs a moment where football fans feel it is about them.

scores.best: A character who looks into the lens and talks to me like a friend is the fastest way to make people love someone, and the format is how this age group really films a trip. 'The Train Home', where she whispers over her sleeping friends, falls asleep herself, and the last shot is filmed by Yuki, is a lovely ending.
scores.worst: A clay figure filming a selfie is a gimmick I would have to explain, and the three camera modes (selfie, flip, handed over) add a 'who is filming now?' question on top of the story. The whole series hangs on one voice, and voices changing was a screw-up of the first series; the selfie arm is the kind of thing that comes out with rubber fingers. The pilot's turn is the weakest of the suitcase stories: she is simply tired, and the authors themselves admit it may not read with the sound off. It has the most talking and reading of the five.
scores.steal: The squeezed group selfie as a signature last frame: three laughing faces pushed into one picture, as if the friends took it themselves. It could close every film or serve as the cover image without making the whole series a vlog.

advice:
Away Crew is the one I would make, but it is an 8 and these are the things that would make me fight for it.

1. Show me the look before anything else. I want one line-up still of the three and one 4-second speaking clip. If my first thought is 'kids' show', stop and push further toward designer art-toy and streetwear (longer limbs, smaller eyes, real fabric). No film gets generated until I say yes to that picture.

2. Zero screw-ups is a gate, not a hope. Generate the closing shot first. Lock one voice per character; if a voice is not identical across shots, cut the line and let the picture carry it. Never ship a drifting voice, a black band, a suitcase that changes size or a garbled letter. Reject and redo, do not patch.

3. Prove I will understand it. Before publishing, show each film with the sound off to someone who has seen nothing. If their one sentence does not match the intended retelling, it does not go out.

4. Make it a football trip from the first frame. With no header, the crew scarves must be clearly visible in shot 1 and the stadium must be heard early. Otherwise the pilot reads as a generic holiday until shot 4.

5. Give it one jolt of energy and one lump in the throat. The pilot is nice but soft. Somewhere in the first three films I need a moment as physical as the suitcase ride in the duo. Somewhere in the six I need one emotional film: the first sight of the pitch, or a local giving away his scarf. The fans should feel it, not only smile.

6. Protect Maya. She is wrong in One Night, No Scarf and The Map. Give her a film where her plan saves the day (the 'Just In Case' idea from the duo), so that nobody is the fool and each of the three is the hero in turn.

7. Give people a reason to share. Ask 'Which one are you: Maya, Kofi or Yuki?' in the post text. Keep 'You never know' as Kofi's line in every film so people quote it. Treat the pink-and-yellow scarf as the community's real badge from day one.

8. Keep the reading at zero. Lines stay at 3 to 5 words, one at a time, saying only what I can already see. Use the 'When your friend packs for one night' line in the post text or the cover, not inside the film. Check that 'Next time, bring two' lands with a second-language viewer; if it does not, end on the silent hug.

9. Keep the pilot simple. The ketchup beat stays only if it comes out clean; cut it at the first sign of trouble. End the film on the hug of the suitcase and Kofi's laugh, with nothing added after it.

scores.best: Only two recurring people, so nearly every frame sits inside the zone the brief says works well (one or two people, a reaction face, dragging a suitcase, hugging). The pilot is dry and sunny throughout: no rain, nothing opens, nothing comes out of the suitcase, nothing is handed over, and only two voices have to be locked. Stills start after the hard part (Luna already seated, Timo already on his knees). The rest of the season is the most makeable of the five: Try It, Left or Right and Wake Up Luna are almost all single-person or two-person shots of eating, walking and sleeping.
scores.worst: The whole payoff rests on the hardest clip, the ride in shot 6. Two people cannot plausibly sit on top of an upright chest-high four-wheel case, so the model will bend the prop or the bodies exactly where the viewer is looking. The designs also carry too many one-sided details that image and video models mirror or drop: thin wire glasses, watch on the left wrist, one streak front-left, odd socks, half-tucked shirt, lopsided scarf. Five lip-synced lines in 27 seconds repeat the voice and lip exposure that hurt series one, and several clips (1, 4, 7) hold three or four beats each. Shot 3 has her walking backwards up steps with a heavy case, which models do badly.
scores.steal: Start every still as late as possible, after the difficult action has already happened (already sitting on the case, already kneeling beside it), so the clip only has to animate the easy remainder.

scores.best: Nobody speaks, which removes lip-sync and voice drift outright: two of the four documented slips of series one cannot recur. Gasps and laughs are laid in during the mix, so audio is fully controlled, and the look can be changed without rewriting anything. The last shot is filmed from behind so no face has to match, and a friend who is asleep is the cheapest possible third character to keep stable.
scores.worst: With no words, the comedy depends on exact mime and timing the models do not deliver on command: a single raised eyebrow, going cross-eyed at a raindrop, a thumb under a backpack strap, pats landing on the beat. Several shots are badly overloaded: shot 2 has three people, a backward stair climb, body contact and passing fans in 3 seconds; shot 7 has five people, a cat, an umbrella mounted on a suitcase, pigeons and a group run in one 6-second clip. The umbrella rising from the case is an object changing shape, and rain has to stay consistent across four shots with a composited drop on a moving face. Shot 1 has the suitcase and Timo entering a frame whose start still does not contain them.
scores.steal: Make the series wordless at the picture level: no lip-sync anywhere, all human sound (gasps, laughs, cheers) added in the mix, so no voice can ever change between clips or films.

scores.best: The most disciplined production thinking in writing: a world with no letters, crowds only as colour shapes, the suitcase given its own reference sheet, the closing clip generated first as a go or no-go, and hand-overs written out of the script (cut from the open suitcase to people already wearing ponchos; the ketchup rises in Kofi's own fist). Most shots are one action plus one reaction face, and the payoff is a hug, the easiest strong ending of the five.
scores.worst: Shot 4 asks for a raindrop on a nose, three people looking up together, rain starting mid-clip, a backpack pulled off and held overhead and a fries cone shielded, all in 3 seconds. Shot 5 needs a lid opening on a tidy, specific interior. The ponchos are a second costume on all three that no reference sheet covers, and they paint the whole cast the same yellow, erasing the colour coding that keeps the characters stable. Five lip-synced lines across three voices, including the make-or-break last line spoken with a cheek pressed on the case, plus rain continuity over four shots. The Chant is set in the stand, which contradicts the rule that the stadium is only light and sound.
scores.steal: Write every hand-over as a cut: show the source (open suitcase), then cut straight to the result (people already wearing the ponchos), so no object ever travels between hands on camera.

scores.best: The diary grammar makes jump cuts and wobble feel intended, which hides seams for free, and the two flip shots (2 and 5: one person, one suitcase, seen from a friend's eye height) are the simplest and safest clips in any of the five pilots. Only four spoken lines, and a large face speaking to the lens is a framing where lip-sync tends to hold.
scores.worst: Every story beat is forced through one camera logic, so there are no cutaways, inserts or over-shoulder angles to rescue a failed clip. The wide front-camera look distorts faces, which is the worst condition for keeping a stylised character identical to a reference sheet, and it puts an arm and fingers (a raised single finger, a thumb jerk) right at the lens. The suitcase in shot 4 and Yuki in shot 7 enter frames whose start stills do not contain them, so the model invents them. Shot 6 (riding a chest-high upright case while someone runs behind) followed by a selfie taken from on top of it, with three faces squeezed to a wide lens, is the hardest pair of clips to match. Nina humming the theme cannot be generated in tune.
scores.steal: The flip shot: a single-person point-of-view clip from a friend's eye height looking at one character and one object, used as the safe reaction beat between harder shots.

scores.best: The 12 frames per second conform with light grain is a real finishing tool that hides wobble and pulls mismatched clips into one material. Sami is designed for generation: hood always up and sleeves over his hands, so there is no hair and no fingers to drift, and he is usually asleep.
scores.worst: The pilot is the hardest to make cleanly: a station hall and platform (signs, clocks and a train front invite garbled text), a moving entry through a train door, a fourth speaking character with a whistle and a wrist check, and the centrepiece clip of three figures at full sprint with one riding the case. The final shot seats three people on a one-metre suitcase described elsewhere as fridge-sized, so the size slip is built into the script. Five lines across four voices, a header on screen for the whole film competing with captions, and a football pinned under one specific arm for six films. Later films put a scarf from one person's neck onto another (hand-to-hand at the centre of the story), a river of fans, and the inside of a stadium with a visible pitch.
scores.steal: Conform every film to 12 frames per second with light grain in the edit, so generated wobble reads as stop-motion and all clips share one texture.

advice:
Plan, No Plan wins on production because it has two people, a dry sunny pilot and nothing that opens or changes shape. To make it without visible faults:

1. Rebuild the ride before anything else. Fix on a prop sheet how two people sit on the case (a lower, wider trunk shape, or lying on its back) and approve a "ride pose" still. Shoot the fallback as the main plan: a waist-up two-shot of both faces in the wind with the street streaking past and the wheels out of frame, a one-second low insert of wheels on cobbles, and at most a short wide. Generate this clip first as the go or no-go, then shot 7.

2. Strip the one-sided details. Models mirror and drop them, and that is the "cup that changed hands" slip waiting to happen. Keep one bold mark per person. Make the watch huge and chunky and never specify a wrist in the script. Turn the glasses into thick clay frames or remove them. Drop the odd socks, the half tuck and the front-left streak (use a full coral fringe or a clip). Make both scarves two wide stripes.

3. Cut the lip-sync exposure to two or three lines. Keep "It is one night!" and "I love this suitcase." on large faces. Play "The match starts in five minutes!" from behind the shoulder as written, and turn "No. No, no, no." into a head shake with sound only. Lock both voices from one source before any film clip, and run every line through it. Finish a fully silent cut first and add speech only where the clip is clean.

4. One idea per clip. Shots 1, 4 and 7 each carry three or four beats, so split them or start later. Shot 4's idea (her eyes going to the wheels) is too subtle for generated acting. Replace it with a close insert of the case starting to roll by itself and her hand catching it.

5. Remove the stairs. Use the cobbled slope from the start, with Luna pulling forwards, not walking backwards.

6. Approve all seven start stills side by side before any video: suitcase top level with Luna's chest, full-frame 9:16 with the top eighth free for the header, no letter-like shapes, stadium only as a blur. Reject a bad clip and regenerate it; never patch.

7. Finish with the 12 frames per second conform and light grain so clips share one texture. Retime the pats and bumps onto the beat in the edit, and replace generated wheel and crowd sound with one consistent set.

8. Protect the season with a hard limit of the two leads plus at most one local per frame. Move The Chant out of the stand to a sunlit wall outside the gate. Make the poncho film's rain as sun-streaks added in the edit over dry clips.

films.retell: A guy comes to a one-night trip with a huge orange suitcase and his friend with a tiny backpack thinks he is crazy and has to help push it up the stairs. Then it rains, he opens the suitcase and it is full of yellow rain ponchos (and even ketchup for the third girl's fries), and the friend who laughed at him ends up hugging the suitcase.
films.who_wants_what: The girl with the tiny backpack wants to travel light and wants to know why he brought so much. The suitcase guy just wants to be ready for anything. The fries girl only wants to eat her fries, then wants ketchup.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: The ketchup. She asks 'Do you have ketchup?' and he lifts the bottle without even looking at her. That is the best joke of the film. The warm part is the last shot: the same girl who was shocked now hugs the suitcase and says 'Next time, bring two.' The good-dog pat in shot 2 is cute too.
confused: Shot 3: a girl sits at the top of the stairs eating fries. Nobody told me who she is. I thought she was a stranger until she stood with them in shot 4.
Shot 4: I did not understand where they are or where they are going. The stadium is only blurry lights, so with no sound I did not know it is a football match. For me it was just 'a square'.
Shot 5: he looks up 'past the camera' with the poncho. At who? I guessed at the girls, but I do not see them.
Shot 6: the suitcase girl's friend with the backpack is suddenly not in the picture. And the ketchup comes from below the frame, so I had to guess it came from the suitcase.
End card: a pink-and-yellow scarf lies under the word. I never saw this scarf in the film, so it means nothing to me. And I do not know what VENUVOY is. A travel company? A suitcase brand?
films.would_follow: Maybe. The story is clear and the ketchup joke made me smile, so I would watch one more. But I do not know what the account is about, and the middle (stairs, rain) is a bit slow and ordinary. I only know one name (Kofi) because it is in the caption.

films.retell: A girl films herself on a one-night trip and laughs that her friend Otto brought a giant yellow suitcase. Later she is too tired to walk, he rolls the suitcase to her, she sits on it and he pushes her down the street, and she says she loves the suitcase.
films.who_wants_what: The selfie girl wants to move fast and make fun of the suitcase. Otto wants to keep his suitcase and prove it is useful. The third girl only eats.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: Shot 6, when she rides on top of the suitcase with her arms up and he runs behind pushing. It looks like real friends having fun. The repeated two pats on the suitcase are a nice small thing. But I did not really laugh anywhere.
confused: Top line and shot 1 say the same thing twice (one night, giant suitcase). Not confusing, just repeated.
Shot 3: a second girl with a pastry is suddenly there. Who is she? Also the girl taps her wrist with no caption: are they late? Late for what? I never find out where they are going.
Shot 4: one shot ago she was fresh and jumping and Otto was the tired one. Now she is finished and sitting on the road. The jump was too fast, I had to guess a lot of time passed.
Shot 5: no caption. He pats the suitcase and lifts his eyebrows. I had to guess he means 'sit on it'. I only understood for sure in shot 6.
Whole film: 'You never know' made me wait to see what is inside the suitcase. It is never opened. So that line does not really pay off, the suitcase is just a seat.
Shot 7: Otto points his thumb at himself. I guess it means 'I told you'. Not sure.
End card: I do not know what VENUVOY is, and in this film there is no sign of football or any place they go to.
films.would_follow: Probably not from this one alone. It is nice and looks young and real because of the selfie style, but it is soft. Nothing big happens, there is no real problem, and the joke is weaker than in the others. I would scroll on after one watch.

films.retell: A girl with a tiny backpack has to help her friend push a giant pink suitcase up a whole hill town, and even a fat cat walks faster than them. Then it rains hard, a huge striped umbrella jumps out of the suitcase and covers everybody, she hugs the suitcase, and they all roll and then run to the stadium under it.
films.who_wants_what: The girl wants to get up the hill without this stupid heavy suitcase. The suitcase guy is relaxed and just wants his suitcase with him. Everyone is walking to a football match (I understood this only from the lights and the end card).
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: The cat. It walks past them, looks back at her and flicks its tail. That is really funny with no words at all. The umbrella shooting out of the suitcase is a good surprise, and the coloured light on their faces sounds beautiful. Warm: he makes room for two strangers under the umbrella, and the cat rides on top, dry.
confused: Shot 2: a third girl climbs with her eyes closed and a travel pillow, holding the backpack. Who is she, and why is she asleep while walking? I accepted it as a joke but nobody explains it.
Shot 2 and 3: people in orange scarves and tall light masts far away. I had to guess this is football. With basic eyes it could be any town.
Shot 5: he pats the suitcase twice in the rain. Without sound I did not know why. It only made sense after the umbrella.
Shot 6: the pole 'shoots up' out of the suitcase by itself. Nobody presses a button. Is it a magic suitcase? A real product? I liked it but I did not understand how.

Shot 7: too many things in one shot: cat on top, two new fans, pigeons, the sleeping girl wakes, everybody runs. With no sound I did not know WHY the birds fly and why they suddenly run. I guessed a goal or the match starting. This was the moment I was most lost.
Shot 7: when did the cat get on the suitcase? It was on a wall three shots ago.
End card: text over a moving picture, and I still do not know what VENUVOY is. 'Next match' tells me football, that is all.
films.would_follow: Yes, maybe. This is the one that works best for someone with weak English because there is nothing to read, and the cat and the umbrella are the two pictures I would remember. But the ending is a mess without sound, and it is fuller and more complicated than it needs to be.

films.retell: Three friends are late for the train on their first football trip and one of them cannot pull his fridge-size yellow suitcase. The girl gets an idea: they put the third friend, who is asleep on his feet, on top of the suitcase and push it together at full speed past a laughing train guard into the train.
films.who_wants_what: The girl wants to catch the train. Otto wants the same but his suitcase is too heavy. The sleepy guy wants only to sleep. The guard wants to close the door on time but she is kind and waits.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: The last shot: the sleeping guy opens one eye, says 'Are we there?' and falls asleep again on Otto's shoulder. That is the real laugh. The guard laughing and waving them in is warm. The sleeping guy smiling on top of the flying suitcase is a good picture.
confused: Top line: 'Mission 1' is nice, it sounds like a series. No problem here, I understood the goal fast.
Shot 3: a new guy with a hood and a ball walks with closed eyes. Who is he? Why is he asleep while walking? I had to accept it.
Shot 3: why did Otto bring a suitcase as big as a fridge? No one says anything about it. In the other films this is the joke, here it is just there.

Shot 4 to 5: this is my biggest problem. The caption says the suitcase is TOO HEAVY. Then her idea is to put a whole person on top, so it is heavier, and now it flies? I guessed the idea is 'two people push and the slow sleepy one rides', but the picture does not say that. I had to think about it, and thinking kills the joke.
Shot 6: they pass as a colour blur. I am not sure I would see that the sleeping guy is still on top.
End card: 'See you at the match' is clear for football, but I do not know what VENUVOY is.
films.would_follow: Maybe. It has the clearest goal (catch the train) and a good last joke, and 'Mission 1' makes me curious about Mission 2. But the idea in the middle is not logical, so the big moment did not hit me as it should.

films.retell: A nervous guy with a watch and a tiny backpack is shocked that his friend Luna brought a giant yellow suitcase for one night, and it makes them late for the match. At the top of a long hill she sits on the suitcase, he says no, and then they both ride it down the street screaming and laughing and arrive on time, and he hugs the suitcase.
films.who_wants_what: He wants to be at the match on time (he keeps tapping his watch). She wants her big suitcase and wants to have fun. In the end the suitcase gives him what he wanted.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: 'No. No, no, no.' and then a hard cut to him on the suitcase screaming with crooked glasses. That made me laugh the most of all five films. His scream turning into a laugh is the warm moment. 'This is the small one!' is also a real joke I understood at once. The end, him on his knees hugging the suitcase, is sweet.
