title: Plan, No Plan
premise: Two best friends travel to football matches abroad: Timo plans every minute and Luna plans nothing. Each film is one small trip problem where his way meets her way; one of them says "No", and one cut later they are both doing it and laughing.
bible:
# PLAN, NO PLAN: series bible

## 1. Premise

Two best friends travel to football matches abroad. Timo plans every minute. Luna plans nothing. Each film is one small trip problem where his way meets her way. One of them says "No", and one cut later they are both doing it and laughing.

Each film is one complete small story of 22 to 30 seconds. Someone who watches one film, once, with the sound off, can say what happened in one sentence.

## 2. Tone

- Sunny, quick, warm and a little cheeky. The two tease each other with some bite and always end closer.
- Friends, never a couple. They push each other, laugh at each other, hang an arm on a shoulder. The big hug of each film goes to the object (the suitcase, the backpack, the food), not to each other. No hand-holding, no long looks.
- Each is right in turn. Her way wins one film, his plan wins the next. Nobody is the fool and nobody is taught a lesson.
- Real fans. They are loud and a bit wild when it matters. Food and coffee, never beer as the joke.
- The town is generous, and the locals they meet are mostly their own age. Making a friend at an away match is part of the dream.
- Voices are natural and low-key: light second-language accents, contractions ("It's one night"), laughs that are not cut clean. Never bright cartoon acting.
- It never feels like a brand: no header line, no slogan, no narrator, no "hey guys".

## 3. The rules that keep every film clear

1. **One sentence first.** Every film starts from its retell sentence: who wants what, what gets in the way, how it pays off. If the sentence cannot be said in one breath, the film is not made.
2. **Two people, known in two seconds.** Tall, teal, big watch, tiny backpack is Plan. Short, coral, hands full is No Plan. No name and no word is needed to tell them apart.
3. **The problem is in frame one.** The first frame shows both friends and the one big object of the film, already in conflict (a tiny backpack beside a giant suitcase). No establishing shot, no title.
4. **One object carries the film.** It is the biggest, brightest thing in frame one (the suitcase, the flatbread, the poncho, the scarf rail). First it is the problem, then it is the answer. A viewer who watches only that object can follow the story.
5. **The watch is the clock.** Timo's big yellow watch shows time pressure with no number: a finger on the watch means hurry, hands on the head mean late, a look at it and a smile mean they made it.
6. **One idea per shot.** A shot is held at least 3 seconds and at most two things happen in it. If a shot needs a third "then", it is split or it starts later.
7. **Cause you can see, in order.** Slow uphill, fast downhill. The answer comes out of the problem object in front of the camera; we never cut to a result with no visible link.
8. **Only the story is on screen.** A film has the two friends, at most one local, and the cat for one shot. A local gets a clear first moment alone in the frame before doing anything. Nobody appears unexplained in the background.
9. **Every sound that matters has a picture.** A roar is also bunting shaking or arms going up. Drums are also a drummer or a stream of scarves moving one way. Nothing important is only heard.
10. **Words are a bonus.** At most one short spoken line per shot (3 to 5 words, never more than 10) that names what the picture already shows. Every film is cut and approved silent first.
11. **One text at a time.** The only text is the caption of the line being spoken. No header, no second line, and no sign, screen, letter or number inside the picture.
12. **The last frame answers the first.** Same framing, opposite feeling (shock at the suitcase, then a hug for the suitcase). The payoff is an action on a face. It is never a caption, a sound or the end card.
13. **Each film stands alone.** No recap, no joke that needs an earlier film, no cliffhanger.
14. **Two gates before release.** (a) The start pictures of all shots, laid side by side like a comic strip with no text, must tell the story. (b) The finished film is shown once, muted, on a phone, to a young viewer and to an adult with English as a second language, who have seen nothing. It is released only if their one sentence matches ours.

## 4. Cast

### Timo, 23: "Plan"
Very tall and thin (about 190 cm), long legs and arms, stands very straight. Dark brown skin, long oval face, high cheekbones, big round dark-brown eyes, thick straight eyebrows that tilt up in the middle when he worries, a wide mouth with a shy smile, clean-shaven. Black tight curls in a short neat flat-top with sharp edges. No glasses.
Always wears: a deep teal retro track jacket, zipped up, collar standing, one cream stripe down each sleeve; straight dark navy trousers that end above the ankle; cream socks; clean white trainers; a small square teal backpack high on both shoulders; a huge chunky sunflower-yellow watch with a blank face, worn over the jacket cuff so it always shows. Trip scarf knotted once at the throat, both ends the same length.
Who he is: he has planned every minute and loves being early. He is the bigger football fan of the two and missing kick-off is his only real fear. He moves in straight lines, quick and exact. When the plan breaks he freezes for one beat with his eyebrows up, says no, and then enjoys it more than anyone. Gentle, never bossy, first to laugh at himself.
Voice (locked): soft, quick, light tenor, light non-native accent.

### Luna, 22: "No Plan"
Short and sturdy (about 158 cm, she reaches his shoulder), strong legs, weight on one hip, never quite still. East Asian features, warm light-tan skin, round face with full cheeks, dark eyes that close into crescents when she laughs, short straight eyebrows, a very wide grin. Black blunt bob to the chin, always a little messy, with the whole fringe dyed coral.
Always wears: an oversized plain coral retro football shirt with a cream collar and cream cuffs, worn loose; baggy light-blue denim shorts to the knee; cream socks pulled up; chunky cream trainers, scuffed, laces loose. Trip scarf loose round her neck, not knotted, both ends hanging down her front.
Who she is: says yes to everything, plans nothing, and somehow it works. Always hungry, always a little late, never worried. She moves in curves, towards food, music and animals. Big laugh with her head thrown back. Half of whatever she is eating belongs to whoever stands next to her. She knows she would miss every train without him.
Voice (locked): low, a little husky, loud, laughs in the middle of words, light non-native accent.

### The cat (working name Mango, never named on screen)
A fat ginger street cat with a cream chest and paws, a short thick tail and half-closed green eyes. It owns the town. In one shot per film it does with no effort what the two friends are struggling to do, looks at them once and walks on. It is never needed to understand the story.

### The yellow suitcase (a prop with its own reference sheet)
Shiny sunflower-yellow hard shell, rounded corners, raised ridges down the front, four black wheels, one black pull handle. About the size of a washing machine: the lid is level with Luna's elbow and Timo's hip, so she can lean an elbow on it and both can sit on it. No stickers, straps or letters. It appears on travel days only and it never goes inside a stadium.

### Locals
At most one per film, mostly their own age (a scarf seller, a fan with a drum, a waiter), drawn in the same style, in plain lilac home scarves. Always the generous one, never the joke.

### The trip scarf
Wide teal and coral blocks with a cream fringe: his colour and her colour on one scarf, a pair that belongs to no club. Both wear it clearly in the first frame of every film, and it lies under the name on the end card. It is the badge of the series.

## 5. World and look

STYLISED, not photoreal. The friends look like collectible designer art-toy figures in real miniature streetwear, in a sunny hand-built model town, filmed as if a friend holds the camera.

- Figures: adult proportions with long legs, heads only slightly larger than life, eyes smaller than a cartoon's, thick eyebrows that do the acting, simple chunky hands, hair as solid sculpted shapes. Matte soft skin with a slight handmade texture. Clothes are real fabric at toy scale (knit, felt, denim, nylon) with a visible weave. Trainers are scuffed. This is something a 23-year-old collects, not something a five-year-old watches.
- World: one invented football town on a hill. Painted houses in cream, terracotta, mint and sky blue, cobbled streets, plain cream bunting, lemon trees in pots, low walls. No letters or numbers anywhere: signs are plain colour shapes and simple pictures. The stadium is a cream bowl with four floodlight masts, seen from outside in the distance or as a bright glow. Crowds are soft shapes of colour. The match itself is never shown.
- Palette: cream base, teal for Timo, coral for Luna, sunflower yellow only for his watch and her suitcase, lilac for home fans. Shadows are warm violet. No black, no grey.
- Light: always sun. Golden late afternoon is standard, pink-gold for mornings, rain only as a sun-shower. Interiors are flooded with sun from a big window. Never night, never a dim room.
- Camera: eye level, close to faces, a small handheld wobble, one simple move per shot, soft backgrounds. Full-frame 9:16. Faces sit in the upper two thirds and the lower middle stays calm for the caption.
- Finish: one warm grade and light grain on every film. Character motion is stepped to 12 pictures per second in the edit for a stop-motion feel that hides generated wobble; this is decided once, at the look test, by showing the same clip both ways on a phone.
- One locked outfit per friend, for ever.

## 6. Music theme

One theme made for the series, about 120 beats per minute, so a beat is half a second and every cut lands on a beat. Warm afro-house with an amapiano bounce, major key. It leads with a log-drum bass and shaker and must knock on a phone speaker.

- Timo's sound: a dry tick-tock on woodblock and muted marimba, exactly on the beat, like a watch.
- Luna's sound: the loose log drum with a cowbell that lands a little late.
- The hook: a five-note "oh-oh-oh" sung by three or four young voices, rough and slightly out of tune like friends in a stand, plus three hand claps. It is used only on the payoff.
- Shape in every film: tick-tock and shaker from frame one, with no intro. The log drum comes in with the obstacle. The music dips under each spoken line. On the "No" everything drops to the tick-tock alone. On the hard cut the full groove and the "oh-oh-oh" land together. The last three claps hit the end card.
- Natural sound is as loud as the music and comes from one consistent sound set: wheels on stone, a far crowd, wind, laughter that is not cut clean.
- Never: whistling, ukulele, stomp-clap advert music, trailer drums, whoosh effects, a trending sound.

## 7. Captions

- The only caption is the line being spoken in that shot: 3 to 5 everyday words, on screen for the whole shot.
- Large bold sans-serif, sentence case, lower-middle safe area, plain white with a soft shadow, like the platform's own text.
- One text at a time. No header line, no coloured highlight word, no emoji, no word-by-word pop.
- A shot with no spoken line has no caption. If a line is cut, its caption goes with it.
- Every film is checked once with all text covered. It must still tell the story.

## 8. The shape of a film

Five to seven shots, 22 to 30 seconds, always in this order:

1. **The clash (3 to 4 seconds).** Frame one: both friends and the one big object, his way against her way.
2. **It gets worse (one or two shots).** The object makes trouble. The cat may pass here.
3. **The squeeze (3 to 4 seconds).** The clock runs out, and the idea appears as something that physically happens (the suitcase starts to roll downhill by itself).
4. **The No (3 seconds).** One of them refuses: shakes the head, shows both palms, steps back. "No. No, no, no." The music drops to the tick-tock.
5. **The cut (4 to 5 seconds).** A hard cut to both of them doing exactly that thing. A scream turns into a laugh. The full theme lands. This is the frame people screenshot.
6. **The answer (4 to 5 seconds).** Frame one again with the feeling turned round. Someone hugs the object. Both laugh, and the laugh is not cut clean.
7. **End card (1.5 seconds).**

Who says the No changes from film to film, and so does who turns out to be right.

## 9. What never happens

- Nothing that must be read: no header, sign, screen, phone, chat, ticket, document or counter. No narrator.
- No irony, no deadpan, no subtext, no joke that needs another film, no cliffhanger.
- Nobody is humiliated. The local and the fan who does not know the chant are never the target.
- No romance between the two.
- No third recurring human, no figure who appears unexplained, no more than two friends plus one local in a frame.
- No night, no dim room, no grey grade.
- No crowd in focus, no match action, no inside of the stadium beyond light, green glow and sound. The suitcase never enters a stadium.
- No object passed from hand to hand on camera: every hand-over is a cut. No precise hand work, no mirrors.
- No real club, badge, kit colour pair, stadium, city, player or brand. Never the word "soccer". No national stereotypes.
- No alcohol as the joke, no aggression, no rival fans as enemies.
- No slang of one country and no line longer than ten words.
- No logo, app, price, slogan or call to action. No talking to the camera, no selfie-vlog shots.
- No trending sound or meme format.
- No film posted without the platform's AI label.

## 10. End card

About 1.5 seconds on a plain warm cream card: the word VENUVOY in the middle, the teal-and-coral trip scarf lying flat under it like an underline, and one small line below: "See you at the next match." The last three claps of the theme land on it. No logo animation, no app, no link. The card cuts straight back to frame one, so the film loops.

## 11. Around the film (cover and post text)

- The line "When your friend packs for one night" lives on the cover image and in the post text, never inside the film.
- The post asks one question: "Plan or No Plan. Which one are you?" We never write "tag your friend"; if the characters are right, the comments do it.
- Two or three hashtags at most. The AI label is always on.
- What Venuvoy is belongs in the account name and bio, not in the films.

episodes.title: One Night
episodes.story: Timo wants to reach the match on time, but Luna's giant suitcase makes them slow all the way up the hill. At the top she sits on it, he says no, and one cut later they ride it down to the stadium, make it, and he hugs the suitcase.

episodes.title: Just In Case
episodes.story: A sun-shower catches them on the walk to the stadium; Timo pulls a rain poncho over his head from his tiny backpack, shows Luna a second one, and she looks at the ugly thing and says no. One cut later she is dancing through the rain in it and hugging his tiny backpack.

episodes.title: Try It
episodes.story: Timo wants to eat the neat sandwiches he brought from home and shakes his head at the huge, messy street flatbread Luna holds under his nose. One cut later he has a flatbread in each hand and sauce on his chin, and she is happily finishing his sandwiches.

episodes.title: No Scarf
episodes.story: Timo already has a scarf and a second one is not in the plan, so he says no to the smiling scarf seller while Luna holds one up to his face. One cut later he walks away in three scarves, a hat and a flag as a cape, prouder than anyone, and Luna has to run to keep up.

episodes.title: One Beat Late
episodes.story: Outside the gate the fans clap a rhythm: Timo knows it but claps tiny and shy, and Luna claps huge and at the wrong moment, arms down when everyone's are up. A local fan their age shows them big and slow, Timo says no, and one cut later he is clapping over his head, the loudest of all, with Luna finally in time beside him.

episodes.title: Same Face
episodes.story: Timo wants to be inside before kick-off, but at the foot of the endless stadium stairs Luna sits down with her food and says no. One cut later he is pulling her up by both hands, and on the last step they both stop dead in the green light with exactly the same open-mouthed face.

episodes.title: No Voice
episodes.story: The morning after the match they want breakfast on a sunny terrace, but neither has a voice left: mouths open, hands go to throats, nothing comes out. Luna orders eggs by flapping like a chicken, Timo shakes his head without a sound, and one cut later he is flapping too, while the waiter, who has no voice either, flaps back and points at his own scarf.

episodes.title: Wake Up, Luna
episodes.story: At sunrise Timo is dressed and wants to catch the early train, but Luna pulls the blanket over her head and says no. One cut later she walks down the sunny street wrapped in the blanket with her eyes shut, following the warm pastry he holds in front of her nose, and on the train she is wide awake eating it while he sleeps sitting bolt upright.

production_notes: ORDER OF WORK (nothing is generated out of this order): (1) reference sheets for Timo, Luna, the suitcase and the cat: front, side, back and five expressions for each friend; the suitcase standing beside both friends for scale; one 'ride pose' still of both sitting on it. (2) LOOK GATE: one line-up still of the two friends with the suitcase, plus one 4-second speaking clip per friend, shown to the client and to three people aged 18 to 25. (3) STRIP GATE: all seven start stills side by side with no text. (4) Shot 6, then shot 7, generated first as go or no-go. (5) The other five clips. (6) A fully silent cut. (7) Voices. (8) RETELL GATE. (9) Publish with the platform's AI label on.

LOOK GATE, two questions only: 'Who is this made for?' and 'What are these two to each other?'. If anyone answers 'kids', fix the still, not the video: longer limbs, smaller eyes, more real fabric and scuffs, less toy gloss. If most answer 'a couple', first re-pose the still as mates (side by side, the suitcase between them, her fist on his arm, both laughing); if it still reads as a couple, recast Timo as a tall young woman with the same colours, watch, backpack and scripts. Nothing else in the series changes, because no script depends on gender. No film clip is generated until the client has said yes to this still.

STRIP GATE: lay the seven start stills side by side like a comic strip. A person who has read nothing must be able to tell the story from the strip alone: giant suitcase and shocked friend, slow uphill, stadium far below, she sits on it, both ride it, he hugs it. If a still does not carry its beat, the still is redesigned before any video is made.

CHECKLIST FOR EVERY START STILL: full-frame 9:16 with no band at any edge; faces in the upper two thirds and the lower middle calm for the caption; the suitcase lid level with Luna's elbow; both scarves clearly visible; nothing that looks like a letter or a number anywhere (paint it out in the still, never in the video); the watch on the same wrist as in shot 1; stadium and fans only as soft simple shapes. A still that fails is repainted. A clip that fails is rejected and generated again; it is never patched from another take.

START LATE: every still begins after the difficult action has already happened (suitcase already arriving, Luna already seated, both already riding, Timo already on his knees), so each clip only animates the easy remainder. Each clip is generated at 5 to 6 seconds and trimmed to its length in the edit. No clip is asked for more than two actions.

VOICES AND LIPS: lock one voice per friend from the 4-second test clip and run every later line through the same two voices. Only three lines need lips in sync (shots 1, 2 and 7), each on a large face with one speaker. The line in shot 4 is played from behind and the 'No' in shot 5 is carried by the head shake. The silent cut is finished and approved first; a line is added only where its clip is clean. If a line fails, it is dropped together with its caption. The film is written to work with no words at all.

SOUND AND FINISH: replace generated wheel, crowd and wind sound with one consistent set laid in the edit. Retime the bump in shot 1, the pats in shot 5 and the cut into shot 6 onto the beat. One warm grade and light grain over all clips; the 12-pictures-per-second step is applied only if it passed the look test. Check the top and bottom edge of every clip for bands before it enters the edit.

SHOT 1. Start picture: the suitcase already large in the middle of the frame, half a metre from its stop, Luna's two hands on the handle; Timo close on the right with his watch arm up and one finger on the watch, already looking at the suitcase; floodlight masts soft over the roofs; both scarves clear. What moves: the suitcase rolls the last bit, bumps and wobbles; Timo's eyes climb it and his mouth opens; he speaks. Plan B: if the suitcase bends while rolling, start with it already parked and only wobbling. If the lips are wrong, keep the picture and drop the line and caption; the open mouth already says it.

SHOT 2. Start picture: Luna close, elbow already on the lid, grinning, Timo's shoulder at the edge. What moves: only her free arm goes up and her eyes follow it; she speaks. Plan B: if the raised hand deforms, she pats the lid twice with a flat hand instead. If the line fails, use 2 seconds of the proud grin with no caption and give the spare second to shot 3.

SHOT 3. Start picture: side view, the street rising from left to right; Timo's cheek already flat on the yellow shell, close to the camera; Luna ahead, pulling; the cat already on the wall one step behind them. What moves: the suitcase creeps a hand's width, feet slip, the cat walks through the frame and looks back. Plan B: if the cat or the figures drift, make the shot without the cat (Timo lifts his head and looks at his watch) and let the cat first appear in film 2. If the wheels melt into the cobbles, crop tighter so the wheels are out of frame.

SHOT 4. Start picture: from behind at shoulder height; Timo's hands already on his head; the suitcase between them already a hand's width ahead, starting to roll; the stadium clear and simple at the end of the street (cream bowl, four lit masts, bigger than a blur) with soft colour shapes of fans near it. What moves: the suitcase rolls about a metre away from us; Luna steps after it and lands both flat hands on the lid. Timo's line is recorded separately and laid in; no lips are seen. Plan B: start with Luna already holding the suitcase back by the handle, leaning back with her heels skidding, while it pulls downhill like a dog on a lead. If the stadium grows letters or sharp people, repaint the still before animating.

SHOT 5. Start picture: low front angle; Luna already seated on the lid, grinning; Timo beside the suitcase with both palms already up. What moves: two pats on the lid behind her; his head shakes; one step back. The 'No' is laid in as sound, and the shaking head hides any lip mismatch. Plan B: frame over Timo's shoulder so we see only his shaking head and palms from behind, and Luna's face carries the shot.

SHOT 6, GENERATED FIRST. Start picture: the approved ride-pose still: knees up, both already seated and already moving, hair and scarves blown back, background already streaked, the yellow lid visible under them, wheels out of frame. What moves: the background streams past, small bounces, her arms stay up, his scream turns into a laugh, one fist goes up. Never show getting on, the wheels or the stop. Plan B1: a chest-up two-shot of the two faces in the wind, cut in two pieces at the moment the scream becomes a laugh. Plan B2, only if no take is clean: Luna rides alone with her arms up and Timo runs behind pushing, screaming and then laughing; the story holds. If none of these comes out clean, stop before spending on the other shots.

SHOT 7, GENERATED SECOND. Start picture: the same framing as shot 1; the suitcase standing still in the middle; Timo already on his knees with one arm on it, looking at his watch; Luna already bent over laughing; the entrance as a bright glow with soft shapes. What moves: his smile, the line, both arms round the suitcase, cheek down, eyes shut; her arm drops across his shoulders. He says the line before his cheek touches the suitcase, so the mouth is clear. Plan B: a silent hug with Luna's laugh and no caption; the picture alone answers shot 1. If her arm on his shoulders deforms, she stays bent over laughing with no contact.
END CARD: built in the edit with real type, never generated. The scarf under the name is one designed still. It lasts about 1.5 seconds and holds no moving picture behind the text.

RETELL GATE: show the finished film once, muted, on a phone, to a young viewer and to an adult with English as a second language who have seen nothing (and to the AI test viewer). Ask only 'What happened?'. Release the film only if the answer matches: 'His friend brought a giant suitcase that made them late for the match, so they rode it down the hill, got there on time, and he hugged the suitcase.' Then repeat once with all captions covered.

SMALL QUESTIONS WE ACCEPT: viewers asked how the two stop, why the street is empty and what happens to the suitcase at the gate. The stop stays behind the cut (showing it adds a hard clip and a shot), the street stays empty so the ride reads cleanly, and the suitcase never goes inside: the film ends outside, and the bible keeps it out of every stadium. None of these three stopped any viewer from understanding the story.
decisions: WINNER: 'Plan, No Plan' (the duo), taken as the base. Its pilot was understood best by the cold viewers (10, 9 and 9 out of 10; all three said they would follow), it has the highest judge average (7.25), it is first for making without faults and second for clarity, vibe and client. The client's two hardest complaints were 'I understood nothing' and 'no screw-ups', and this concept answers both best. Title and names (Timo, Luna) are kept.

TWO LEADS, NOT THREE. In all four pilots with a third friend, viewers asked 'who is she?' or 'who is he?', and all three viewers named 'only two people' as the reason the duo was clear. I did not take the trio from 'Away Crew' even though the client and vibe judges ranked that concept first: its pilot was understood less well (8.67), had no physical high point, and carried rain, a lid opening and a second costume.

'TWO IS NOT A CREW' AND THE COUPLE RISK are answered inside two people: friends-not-couple rules in the tone (the big hug goes to the object, no hand-holding, mates' body language), a local their own age in most films, the cat, and the cover line 'When your friend packs for one night'. This risk is not proven away: it is tested at the look gate with the question 'What are these two to each other?', with a concrete plan B (re-pose, then recast Timo as a woman) before any video is made.

NO HEADER LINE (from 'Away Crew', backed by the vibe and client judges). The 'When your friend...' line moves to the cover and post text. This also removes the clash one viewer saw between a header about overpacking and a film about being late: the film is now one idea, the suitcase is the problem and then the answer.

CAPTION DISCIPLINE from 'Away Crew': the only text is the current spoken line, 3 to 5 words, one at a time, held for the whole shot, no coloured words. Five short captions, 21 words in total, none needed to follow the story.

THE WATCH AS THE CLOCK is kept from the duo and made a series rule (finger on watch, hands on head, look and smile). The plot line 'The match starts in five minutes!' became the more natural 'We have five minutes!', spoken from behind so no lips are needed.

THE REFUSAL AND THE HARD CUT ('No. No, no, no.' then the opposite) is made the signature of every film, as the vibe judge asked. Who refuses and who is right rotate, so neither friend becomes the fool: Luna is right in three films, Timo in three, both in two.

PILOT SHOT 4 REBUILT on the make judge's idea: the idea no longer depends on a small look at the wheels; the suitcase visibly starts to roll downhill by itself and Luna catches it. The stadium is drawn larger and clearer because one viewer only understood it through the caption.

PILOT SHOT 3 CHANGED: the stairs became a cobbled slope (stairs and walking backwards generate badly), and Timo now pushes with his cheek on the suitcase instead of standing at the top tapping his watch, because a viewer found him annoying for not helping.

KEPT 'This is the small one!' although the clarity judge wants no joke that lives only in a line: it was called the funniest line of all five pilots, and the series needs quotable lines to feel like friends. It is now doubled by a gesture (her hand held high above her own head), and the film loses nothing if the line is cut.

DESIGNS STRIPPED of one-sided details on the make judge's advice: no glasses, a whole coral fringe instead of one streak, matching socks, no half tuck, a scarf of wide blocks, the watch worn over the cuff with no wrist named in any script. Timo's zipped track top is kept as football terrace style so he is neat, not uncool.

THE SUITCASE RESIZED to washing-machine size (lid at Luna's elbow) so two people can plausibly sit on it, and the ride is filmed from the knees up with the wheels out of frame. The ride clip is generated first as the go or no-go, then the closing shot (the 'closing clip first' rule from 'Away Crew').

LOOK: the phrase and direction from 'Away Crew': collectible art-toy figures in streetwear with adult proportions, not clay puppets, plus its world without letters. The trip scarf as the badge of the series (worn clearly in frame one, lying under the name on the end card) is the client judge's steal, in the duo's own teal and coral.

FROM 'Trip Trip Hooray': the rule that every sound that matters has a picture, the muted retell gate before release, the silent-cut-first working method, and the street cat for one shot per film. Rejected: a fully wordless series (the judges said mute puppets read as mascots or children's television with nothing to quote) and the umbrella that shoots out of the suitcase (cartoon magic that viewers could not explain).

FROM 'First Away': the comic-strip gate of start stills, the 12-pictures-per-second finish (as a tested option, not a certainty, because the vibe judge warned it can read as children's television), and the season's emotional image of the pitch opening at the top of the stairs, turned into the film 'Same Face'. Rejected: the 'Mission 1' header, four characters, the station and train doors, and the illogical 'too heavy, so add a person' fix.

FROM 'Match Day Diary': nothing structural. The selfie format and the selfie last frame are rejected: an arm at the lens and a wide lens distort faces, three camera modes made viewers ask who is filming, and the pilot must end on the hug with nothing added after it.

FROM 'Away Crew' films: 'No Voice' (called the best episode idea in the pack) and every hand-over written as a cut. Rejected: Kofi's line 'You never know', because it promises that the suitcase will be opened and viewers of another pilot felt cheated when it was not; and the poncho pilot. The poncho idea survives as film 2, where Timo's plan is the hero.

EPISODES: dropped 'Left or Right' (it cross-cuts two places and splits the two friends, which breaks the clearest thing about the series). 'The Chant' moved out of the stand to a wall outside the gate and is told with arms up and arms down, not with sound. No film hangs on a roar alone. The stadium stays light, glow and sound in every film.

MUSIC: the duo's two motifs are kept, but led by the log drum, with a few rough voices and the hook only on the payoff, to stay away from stomp-clap advert music as the vibe judge warned. The tempo is set to 120 so cuts fall on half-second beats.

END CARD: plain card, 1.5 seconds, no picture moving behind the text. Every viewer asked what VENUVOY is; the brief allows the brand only to sign, so the film does not explain it. The line 'See you at the next match' says football, and the account name and bio say the rest.

NOTHING HERE HAS BEEN GENERATED OR TESTED YET. The look, the couple question, the ride clip and the muted retell are gates with a stated plan B, not results. Only one suitcase film is made, so the viewers' warning about five versions of the same joke and reused names does not apply.

films.retell: A girl, Luna, arrives in a football town with a giant yellow suitcase for only one night, and her tall friend Timo is stressed about the time. They push it up a hill very slowly, see the stadium far down the other side with five minutes left, so they sit on the suitcase and ride it down the street, and they arrive on time and he hugs the suitcase.
films.who_wants_what: Timo wants to get to the stadium on time (he keeps looking at his watch) and thinks the suitcase is a stupid problem. Luna just wants to have fun and bring her huge suitcase, and she wants Timo to get on it and ride down with her. In the end the suitcase he hated is the thing that saves him.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: Funniest for me: the fat cat that walks past them on the wall and is faster than them (shot 3), and 'This is the small one!' with her hand above her head (shot 2). The ride in shot 6 is the best picture: he screams, then the scream turns into a laugh and he puts his fist up. Warm part: at the end he hugs the suitcase with his eyes closed and she puts her arm on his shoulders. The 'No. No, no, no.' and then a hard cut to him already riding is a good, simple joke, even if I saw it coming from shot 4.
confused: Shot 1: A lot happens in 4 seconds: the suitcase rolls in, the watch, his eyes going up, the caption, the scarves. I understood 'big suitcase for one night', but I did not know yet where they are going or why he points at the watch. The floodlights are far away and small; on a phone I would probably not see them, so 'football' was not clear to me here.
Shot 1: 'It's one night' - one night where? I guessed they are on a short trip to this town. Nothing tells me this, I only guess from the suitcase and the train station.
Shot 2: The hand high above her head - I had to think for a second. I guessed it means 'the big one is this tall'. It works, but it is only 3 seconds and I am also reading the caption.

Shot 4: 'We have five minutes!' - five minutes until what? I guessed the match starts, because of the stadium. It is never said. Also with no sound and the two seen from behind, I do not see who says it; I guessed Timo because of his hands on his head and the watch before.

Shot 4: Too many things in one shot: the stadium view, the caption, the suitcase starting to roll alone, Luna catching it. I think I would catch the caption and the stadium and maybe miss that the suitcase rolled by itself, and that is the thing that gives her the idea.

Shot 6 to shot 7: I never see how they stop. One moment they fly down the hill, next moment the suitcase stands still at the stadium. I wanted to see the stop or a small crash. It feels like one piece is missing.
Shot 7: He looks at the watch and smiles - I guessed this means they made it on time. No caption says it. It is an easy guess, but it is a guess.
Shot 7: Small thought: are they going into the stadium with a suitcase the size of a washing machine? Nobody answers this. Not a big problem, but I thought about it.

End card: VENUVOY - I do not know what this is. A travel company? A fan club? An app? The card is 1.5 seconds and tells me nothing. 'See you at the next match' made me guess it is something about going to football games, but I do not know what they do or why I should care.
General: I do not know if they are friends, a couple, or brother and sister. It does not hurt the story, but I did not know.
films.would_follow: Maybe, not from this one video alone. I liked the two of them and I would watch one more if it showed up, mostly for Luna and the suitcase. But I do not know what Venuvoy is or what the account is about, so I have no real reason to press follow yet. If the next one is the same two people and as easy to understand, then yes.

films.retell: Two mates get off the train in a football town for a one-night trip, and the short one, Luna, has brought a yellow suitcase the size of a washing machine, which horrifies the tall, watch-checking one. They drag it up a steep hill so slowly that a cat overtakes them, realise at the top they have five minutes, ride the suitcase down the hill to the stadium, make it in time, and he ends up hugging the thing he was moaning about.
films.who_wants_what: The tall guy (I only know he is called Timo from the description, nobody says his name) wants to be on time and travel light; he is the planner with the watch and the tiny backpack. Luna wants to bring her ridiculous suitcase and is not bothered about anything. From shot 4 they both want the same thing: to reach the ground before kick-off.
films.the_funny_or_warm_part: The cat strolling past them on the wall and looking back (shot 3) is the best joke, and it needs no words. 'This is the small one!' is a good line. The warm bit is shot 6, when his scream turns into a laugh and he punches the air, and then 'I love this suitcase' pays off the first line. Everyone has a mate who overpacks, so the opening is relatable and I would not swipe on it. It is 'aww, nice' funny, not laugh-out-loud; from the moment she pats the lid in shot 5 I knew exactly how it would end.
confused: Shot 1: he has a finger on his watch while complaining about the suitcase size. Two ideas at once (late + overpacked) in 4 seconds. I only understood the watch meant 'we are in a hurry' in hindsight, at shot 4.

Shot 1-3: nobody says where they are going or that there is a deadline. I guessed 'to the match' from the floodlights and the scarves, but for the first 11 seconds there are no stakes; the uphill push in shot 3 is just two people pushing a case.

Shot 2: the flat hand held above her head. I guessed she means 'the big one is this tall', but she looks up at her hand, then at him, then grins, all in 3 seconds. Got it, but it was a guess for a beat.

Shot 3: why are they taking a giant suitcase towards the stadium at all instead of dropping it at a hotel or a locker? Anyone who travels to matches thinks this straight away. I accepted it as cartoon logic, but it nagged.

Shot 4: 'We have five minutes!' Five minutes to what? Kick-off is never said, I assumed it. Also the line comes from behind so I do not see who is talking; I guessed it was him because of the hands on the head.

Shot 4: very crowded. Stadium reveal, hands on head, the line, the suitcase rolling off on its own, Luna jumping and catching it, all in 4 seconds. I could miss that the suitcase rolling by itself is what gives her the idea.
Shot 5: she is suddenly 'already sitting' on it right after catching it with both hands. Small jump, I filled it in.

Shot 6 to 7: there is no stop. One moment they are roaring downhill, the next the suitcase is standing still and he is kneeling beside it. I expected a crash or a landing gag and felt a beat was missing.

Shot 7: they are at the entrance with a washing-machine-size case. No ground lets in a bag bigger than A4. That is the first thing I would write in the comments. Also I never find out what is in it or why it is so big, which felt like an unused joke.
Shot 7: he looks at his watch and smiles, so I assume they made it, but nothing confirms the match has not started (no whistle, no clock). Guessed.

End card: I do not know what VENUVOY is or does. 'See you at the next match' and a scarf tells me football and trips, nothing more. It did not feel like an advert, which I liked, but I also do not know what I would be following.

Whole film: the town, the club and the scarf are invented and the fans are 'soft shapes'. No real ground, no chants, no real colours. It reads as a cute cartoon about a suitcase more than as football away-day culture, so the football part did not hit me personally.
films.would_follow: Not from this one clip alone. I would watch it to the end, probably let it loop once, and tap the profile to see if there are more of these two. If there were three or four more at this level I would follow. What holds me back: it is sweet but safe, the football feels generic (invented town, no real match-day detail), and I have no idea what Venuvoy actually is.

shots.why: The densest shot, and it is the opening. Four beats in 4 s (roll, bump and wobble, eyes climb and mouth drops, line), against the notes' own limit of two actions. Fault points, most likely first: (a) Lip sync with two faces in frame: Luna grins with an open mouth while Timo, turned towards the suitcase, speaks in three-quarter or profile view. The line can land on her mouth, on both, or come out mushy straight after a gaping mouth. (b) A rigid shiny box rolling on four small wheels over cobbles and then bumping: wheels slide or melt, the shell goes rubbery. The wheels are in view because his eyes start there. (c) One finger on the watch, close to a wide lens: a large foreground hand, the finger can fuse with the watch, and a watch face that someone looks at tends to grow hands or numerals. (d) A station front invites a clock, a sign and a timetable. Continuity: this shot fixes the watch wrist, the handle state, the sun side and coral-left / teal-right for the whole film, and it is also the loop point. The reference sheet has the watch on his left wrist, so this still must agree with the sheet or the references will fight each other in every later shot.
shots.safer: Keep the half-metre roll only if the wheels sit below the bottom edge of the frame; otherwise make Plan B the plan (already parked, one last wobble; the rattle and bump are laid in the edit, so the arrival still reads). Give Luna a closed-mouth smile while he speaks and turn Timo's face three-quarters to the camera. The finger is already resting on the watch in the still and never lifts; the watch face is blank and angled slightly away from the lens. The station is a plain arch with no clock.

shots.why: The kind of shot that works best: one person, close, one short line. What is left is small. Four beats in 3 s (hand up, look up, look at Timo, grin plus five words), so the line may be spoken while the head tilts and turns, which is where lip sync slips. A flat hand raised high above her head in a close frame reaches the top edge, and a hand that leaves and re-enters the frame comes back deformed. The teal shoulder at the edge is a partial figure that the model likes to complete or move; at Timo's real height it sits level with her head and shows collar, stripe, scarf and backpack strap, each of which can change. Continuity: he must be on the right edge as in shot 1, the handle in the same state, and the sun from the same side.
shots.safer: Start one beat later: the still already has her hand flat above her head, inside the frame with headroom, and her eyes already on Timo. The clip is only one small bounce of the hand, the line and the grin. Keep Timo as a soft, out-of-focus teal shape on the right edge that does not move.

shots.why: The most loaded shot: three characters that must all stay themselves and five actions (pull, push and slip, cat walks through, cat looks back, eyes follow). Four weak spots at once: a four-legged walk on short legs (legs merge or slide), a face tilted and pressed on a shiny shell (the shell mirrors the face and the cheek can sink into it), long legs slipping (crossed or extra legs), small wheels on cobbles. Three problems that no retake fixes: (1) a cat on a LOW wall on the far side walks behind Timo, the suitcase and Luna, is hidden for most of its walk and comes out as a different cat; on the near side it crosses their faces. (2) Plan B 'crop the wheels out' also crops out the slipping feet, which are on the same line. (3) 'Pulls with both hands, leaning forward' means arms stretched behind her back, a pose that comes out twisted. Also, a heavy thing that should hardly move usually comes out rolling easily, which kills the joke, and 'side view' with 'Timo close to the camera' pulls the still in two directions.
shots.safer: Keep the beat, freeze the friends. Both hold a strain pose and move only a hand's width, framed from the knees up so feet and wheels are out of frame (the slipping is heard, not seen). Luna faces the suitcase and leans back as in a tug-of-war, hands in front of her body. Timo's cheek stays flat on the shell as in the still and never lifts; only his eyes move. The only thing that travels is the cat, on a wall whose top is higher than the suitcase lid, in clear space above everyone: it starts level with Timo, ends ahead of Luna, and the one look back is its last move. If two takes fail, use the written Plan B without the cat.

shots.why: It asks for the three things generated video does worst with objects: an object that starts moving with no visible cause (from a still, the model leaves it parked or invents a push), a body lunging after it, and a stop that must happen exactly when two hands land. Typical faults: the suitcase slides as if on ice, shrinks or changes shape as it moves away, passes through her hands, or stops before she touches it. Blocking: seen from behind, Luna's lunge puts her back between the camera and the suitcase, so the catch and the stadium are both covered at the key moment. Other points: all four wheels are in view from behind; small moving fan shapes sharpen into flickering little people; a steep street flattens in a vertical frame, and a suitcase rolling alone on a street that looks flat reads as a ghost; the back of a football shirt invites a number and a name, the backpack a logo patch. The watch is visible on his raised hands: it must be on the same real wrist, which is the opposite screen side from shot 1 (the classic mirror slip). The line from behind is safe only in a true back view; if any cheek or jaw shows and does not move, it looks dubbed.
shots.safer: Make Plan B the plan. The still already has Luna holding the suitcase back by the handle, leaning back with her heels dug in; the suitcase sits a little to one side of her so that both it and the stadium stay visible, pulling downhill like a dog on a lead. The clip is only strain, a small skid, and Timo's hands on his head with one bounce of the shoulders on his line. Fans are still, soft colour shapes (their movement comes from sound). Paint the drop clearly: roofs stepping down, the stadium below eye level. Shirt back and backpack are plain in the still and checked on the last frame.

shots.why: A design fault before any generation: from a low camera in front, the top of the lid cannot be seen and 'behind her' is hidden by her own body, so the two pats, which are the whole invitation, are invisible; the model twists her arm backwards or drops the pat. Then: two characters each doing two different things at once in 3 s; usually only one of them acts, or they copy each other (both shake heads). Timo's face is in full view from below, so four spoken 'No' over a closed or randomly moving mouth shows, even with the head shake; a head shake stepped to 12 pictures a second can also look like a glitch. Two open palms near a low wide lens show every finger and the watch (wrist again). She sits on a wheeled case at the top of a slope and it must not creep. This reverse angle also flips coral-left / teal-right unless the still is designed to keep it.
shots.safer: Raise the camera to Luna's seated eye level and turn it three-quarters, so the empty back half of the lid is in view; she pats it with the hand nearest the camera. Timo starts with palms already up and only shakes his head and steps back. Have him really say 'No, no, no' in the clip (a round open mouth four times is the easiest line to sync and its errors do not show), or use the written Plan B over his shoulder. Keep Luna on the left and Timo on the right.

shots.why: The film depends on it and it stacks the most. (1) An expression change at a set moment (scream to laugh, halfway) plus a fist: models hold the start expression or change at once, so hitting the music is luck. (2) Two bodies on one moving box: legs have no clear place on a top the size of a washing machine, so 'knees up' fills the bottom of the frame with a tangle of four knees; his hands on her shoulders slide or sink into the shirt while they bounce. (3) Luna's raised arms are directly in front of Timo's face and reach the top edge: a covered face returns as a different face, and hands that leave the frame come back deformed. (4) A camera racing backwards makes everything at the frame edges newly invented scenery, large and close, not taken from the still: this is where door numbers, signs, people, cars or a more realistic style enter. (5) 'Hair flying back' contradicts the solid sculpted hair of the look: the model switches to strands and the toy look breaks; her loose scarf ends blow straight into his face. (6) A wide-open scream and laugh are the expressions furthest from the reference sheet, so both faces drift most here. (7) The scream and the whoop from the clip will not be in the locked voices. (8) Stepping a motion-blurred racing background to 12 pictures a second strobes, and the look test (a calm talking clip) does not cover it.
shots.safer: Make Plan B1 the plan and build it from two stills in the same framing. Still A: Timo screaming, both hands on her shoulders. Still B: Timo laughing, fist already up (the arm without the watch). Two clips of about 2.5 s, cut on the beat where the groove lands, so neither clip contains an acting change. In both stills: chest up, the yellow lid only as a wide bar across the bottom (no knees); Luna's arms in a wide V fully inside the frame with Timo's whole face in the gap above her head; hair stays solid and only scarves and shirt flap, her scarf ends blown out to the sides; walls painted as soft bands of colour with no doors, windows or signs. Add the open scream and the open laugh to both expression sheets, and run the 12-picture test on this shot.

shots.why: Six beats in 5 s in one take (look at watch, smile, line, both arms round, cheek down and eyes shut, Luna's arm lands), three times the notes' own limit, so the model reorders them: he speaks into the shell, or hugs before he smiles. Contact faults: arms cannot reach round a box that size, so the arms stretch or the box shrinks; a cheek arriving on shiny plastic; Luna's arm lands on his backpack and scarf, not on shoulders, and melts into them. Lip sync: Luna laughs with an open mouth right beside the speaker, so the line can land on her. Framing: with Timo on his knees and Luna bent over, both faces sit in the middle of the frame, exactly where the caption goes, so 'I love this suitcase.' would cover the hug. The scarf 'blown back over one shoulder' is a one-sided detail, which the wardrobe rule forbids. Walking fan shapes in the glow sharpen into people with scissoring legs, and a stadium entrance invites signs and numbers. Because the framing copies shot 1 and the film loops, any change in suitcase size, handle, watch wrist or sun side shows directly at the loop.
shots.safer: Start later and cut the take in two planned pieces from two stills. 7a (about 2.5 s): Timo on his knees, watch arm resting on the lid, looks up from the watch, the smile spreads, he says the line; Luna is bent over with her face down, hidden by her hair. 7b (about 2.5 s): the still already has both his arms on the suitcase (hands on the two near corners, not all the way round) and his cheek on the lid; the clip only closes his eyes and squeezes, while Luna, laughing, leans her elbow on the lid as in shot 2 and does not touch him. Camera low enough to keep both faces above the caption line; scarf worn as always; fans as still, soft shapes.

overall: VOICES, TWO PIPELINES IN ONE FILM: the lines in shots 1, 2 and 7 come out of the video clips, while the lines in shots 4 and 5 are recorded separately and laid in. The same person will differ in tone, accent and room sound inside 28 seconds, which is the slip the client already complained about. Safer: record all five lines first, in one session, in the two locked voices, and drive the lips in shots 1, 2 and 7 from that audio; put one room tone under all of them.

VOICES, THE SOUNDS THAT ARE NOT WORDS: laughs, a giggle, a gasp, puffing, a scream and a whoop appear in six of the seven shots and are not covered by the voice lock. Luna has only one line, so her laugh IS her voice; Timo's scream turning into a laugh is the peak of the film. Taken from each clip they will be six different people, and voice converters handle screams and laughs badly. Safer: at the look gate, build a small library per friend in the locked voice (her laugh in three sizes, giggle, gasp, whoop; his puffing and scream-into-laugh) and use only that, in every film.

ACCENT: 'a light non-native accent' is not a specification; it drifts from one generation to the next (one line sounds American, the next from somewhere else). Pin it to one approved reference clip per friend, or choose plain international English.

SAME PERSON LOOKING DIFFERENT, WHERE IT WILL HAPPEN: the back view (shot 4), extreme expressions (shot 6), a tilted or pressed face (shots 3 and 7) and small full figures (shot 3). In motion, art-toy stills drift towards generic 3D cartoon (bigger eyes, smoother skin), which is exactly the 'kids' reading the look gate is meant to prevent; the flat-top rounds off; one sleeve stripe becomes three (a brand look); the plain shirt grows a crest or a number; solid hair turns into strands. Safer: add to the reference sheets a plain back view of each friend and the scream and open-laugh expressions, and check the LAST frame of every clip against the sheet, not only the first.

TIMO'S SKIN TONE: dark brown skin in low golden backlight with violet shadows and 'no black' is where models lighten or grey a face differently in every shot, and the warm grade moves it again. Compare his face across the seven stills side by side, and again after the grade.

COLOURS THAT CARRY THE STORY: who-is-who rests on teal, coral and sunflower yellow staying apart. Golden light plus a warm grade pushes yellow and coral both towards orange and teal towards green; in shot 6 the coral shirt sits directly on the yellow lid. Grade against three fixed colour swatches. The shared scarf carries both colours on both friends, so stills built from several references swap the two scarf states: add 'Timo's knotted, Luna's loose' to the still checklist.

THE SUITCASE AS A PROP: its size against the bodies, its ridged face and above all its handle will change between shots. The handle must be up to pull in shots 1 and 3 and cannot be there when they sit on the lid (5, 6) or hug it (7). Decide once on the reference sheet: a fixed short black grab handle that never extends, and add 'handle' to the checklist. Keep the ridges few and wide so that a ridged hard shell does not look like a known luggage brand.

WHO STANDS WHERE, SUN AND WATCH: keep coral on the left and teal on the right in every two-shot (1, 2, 4, 5, 7); the reverse angle between shots 4 and 5 flips them unless the stills are designed to hold it. Shots 4 and 5/6 look in opposite directions, so pick the sun side once (for example low, from screen left) or the faces go from lit to backlit in one cut. The watch stays on his real left wrist as on the reference sheet, which means the opposite screen side in the back view.

LETTERS AND NUMBERS THAT APPEAR DURING A CLIP: the still checklist is good, but the leaks come in motion, in areas the still never showed: the edges of shot 6, the stadium in shots 4 and 7, the watch face when it moves, house numbers on doors, shop signs, the back of the football shirt, the backpack, trainers, a lock on the suitcase. Look through every clip at the frame edges and at the last frame; reject, do not paint.

THE 12-PICTURES-A-SECOND STEP: it cannot be applied to 'character motion' only; it steps the whole frame, including the handheld wobble and the blurred background. Real stop-motion has sharp frames; generated clips have motion blur baked in, so the result can read as a laggy video, and it loosens lip sync. Test it on shot 6 and on one speaking clip, not only on the calm test clip. If it stays: generate the clips with a still camera, step them, then add the handheld wobble smoothly in the edit.
FINE TEXTURE: a visible weave at toy scale, light grain and phone compression together make fabric crawl and shimmer from frame to frame. Keep the weave coarse and soft in the stills.

MUSIC: the script needs exact hit points (tick-tock on frame one, the bump, the two pats, the groove landing on the cut into shot 6, three claps on the card, a clean loop) and layers that drop in and out (thins to bass and shaker, drops to tick-tock alone). One generated mix cannot be thinned, and separated layers carry artefacts, so the theme must be built or delivered in layers. Fix the tempo before the edit: at 120 beats a minute every length in the script falls on a beat (4 s = 8 beats, 3 s = 6, 5 s = 10) and the 1.5 s card is exactly the three claps; at any other tempo the shot lengths must move. The group 'oh-oh-oh' is the part most likely to sound artificial or to grow word-like sounds, and it must not resemble a real club chant. The far-away drums in the natural sound will clash with the track unless they are in its tempo. Remove any music the clips generate themselves. Listen on a phone speaker: log drum and bass disappear there, so tick-tock and claps must carry. The last clap must end dry or the loop clicks.

CAPTIONS: 'lower middle' collides with three things. (1) The platform's own text and buttons cover roughly the bottom fifth and the right edge, so the caption line must sit higher. (2) In shots 1, 4 and 7 that zone is the shiny sunflower-yellow suitcase, and in shot 7 the faces and the hug: the caption needs a solid backing or outline in deep violet (no black), and stills 1 and 7 must be composed around it. (3) The lines in shots 4 and 5 have no visible lips, so their captions must appear exactly on the audio or the viewer cannot tell who speaks. One typeface, one size and one position in every shot.

END CARD: 1.5 seconds for a name plus a six-word line is fast reading for a second-language viewer, the complaint about the first series, and the brief says the brand signs with the name only. Drop the small line, or hold the card for 2 seconds (four beats at 120).

TRIMMING AND BANDS: clips are generated at 5 to 6 seconds and cut to 3 to 5, so ask for the line and the key action in the first half of each clip, or the best part falls outside the cut. Make every start still at the exact pixel size of the video model's 9:16 output; a still of a slightly different shape is the usual cause of a band at the top or bottom.

title: Plan, No Plan
premise: Two best friends travel to football matches abroad: Timo plans everything and Luna plans nothing. In every film one small trip problem meets his way and her way; one of them says "No", and one cut later they are both doing it and laughing.
bible:
# PLAN, NO PLAN: series bible

## Premise
Two best friends travel to football matches abroad. Timo plans everything. Luna plans nothing. In every film one small trip problem meets his way and her way. One of them says "No". One cut later they are both doing it, and laughing.

## Tone
- Warm, sunny, playful. The teasing always ends with both laughing. Nobody is the fool, and each friend is right in turn.
- Friends, never a couple. They behave like brother and sister by choice: no romantic look or touch, ever.
- Football-trip true. Every situation is one a travelling fan knows. Properly loud at a goal, never aggressive.
- No irony, no subtext, no narrator, no brand before the last two seconds.

## The rules that keep every film clear
1. **The sentence first.** Before a script exists, the film is one sentence a twelve-year-old could say after watching once with the sound off. If the sentence needs "because" twice, the idea is too big.
2. **One big thing that turns round.** Each film is built on one large visible object or place whose meaning flips (in the pilot the yellow suitcase: first the problem, then the hero). The story can be followed by watching that thing alone.
3. **The want is in frame one**, as a gesture or a place (a pointing arm, floodlights, food held out), next to the thing that is in the way.
4. **One idea per shot**, at most two actions, held at least three seconds (two short clips of the same idea count together).
5. **Cause and effect are physical and in order** (slow uphill, fast downhill). Nothing is implied. Nothing must be remembered from another film.
6. **Only the story on screen.** The two friends, plus at most one local or the cat. Luna is always on the left, Timo always on the right.
7. **The "No" cut.** Once per film one friend offers their way with a big gesture, the other refuses with head and hands (it reads without sound), and a hard cut shows both already doing it.
8. **Every sound that matters has a picture double.** A roar is also streamers drifting or light on faces. A wrong clap is also two pairs of hands visibly out of step.
9. **Nothing to read in the picture.** The only text is the spoken line of the moment. Never two texts at once, no header. At most four short lines per film, and none of them carries the story: every cut is tested with all text covered.
10. **The last shot is the first shot turned round**, and the payoff is an action, never a caption and never the end card.
11. **Every film stands alone.** No "previously", no numbers, no cliffhanger.
12. **Three gates before anything is published.** Strip gate: the seven start pictures laid side by side tell the story with no text. Silent gate: the muted cut with captions covered is shown to a real viewer of 18 to 25 and to an adult with English as a second language; it goes out only if their sentence matches ours. Fault gate: every clip is checked edge to edge and on its last frame; a faulty clip is made again, never patched.

## Cast
**Timo, 23, the planner.** About 192 cm, thin, long legs, stands very straight. Dark brown skin, long oval face, round dark-brown eyes, thick straight eyebrows that tilt up in the middle when he worries, wide mouth, clean-shaven. Black hair in a short flat-top fade, one solid sculpted shape with sharp edges. No glasses. Always: a plain teal zip-up track jacket closed to the chin with a cream collar and cream cuffs (no stripes, no logo, plain back); cream straight trousers that end above the ankle; clean white trainers; a tiny square teal backpack worn high on both shoulders; a big chunky sunflower-yellow watch with a blank cream face on his left wrist. Trip scarf knotted once at the throat, both ends short and equal. He loves being early, points the way with his whole arm and moves in straight lines. When the plan breaks he freezes, says "No", and then enjoys it more than anyone. Neat means stylish here, not nerdy. Voice: soft, quick, clear light tenor, plain international English.

**Luna, 22, no plan.** About 158 cm (she reaches Timo's shoulder), sturdy, strong legs, weight on one hip, never quite still. East Asian features, warm light-tan skin, round face, full cheeks, a band of freckles across the nose, dark eyes that close into crescents when she laughs, short straight eyebrows, a wide grin with a small gap between the front teeth. Black blunt bob to the chin, slightly messy outline, the whole fringe coral; one solid sculpted shape. Always: an oversized coral retro football shirt with a cream collar and cream cuffs, completely plain front and back; baggy light-blue denim shorts to the knee; two sunflower-yellow socks pulled up; chunky cream trainers, scuffed, laces loose. Trip scarf loose round her neck, both ends hanging long. She says yes to everything, is always hungry and never worried, and drifts towards food, music and animals. Big laugh. Half of whatever she eats belongs to Timo. Voice: low, a little husky, loud, laughs in the middle of words, plain international English.

**Big Yellow, the suitcase.** A rounded sunflower-yellow hard box on four small deep-violet wheels, satin and not mirror-shiny. Its top is level with Luna's chest. Its flat lid is long enough for two people to sit one behind the other. Two wide raised ridges round its middle. One short fixed deep-violet grab handle on the front end; it never extends. No stickers, locks or letters. It has its own reference sheet like a cast member. What is inside is the running question of the series; when it opens in a later film, that is shown as a cut (closed, then already open). It never goes into a stadium: it waits at the bag hut.

**The ginger cat (working name Ref, never said on screen).** A fat ginger street cat with a cream belly and chin, short legs, a thick tail held up like a question mark and half-closed green-gold eyes. The calm local who watches the two visitors and is never impressed. Once or twice per film, never more.

**Locals.** One per film at most, in the same style, often the friends' own age: a food seller, a scarf seller, a fan who knows the clap, a waiter. The local is always the generous one and never the target of a joke.

## World and look
Stylised, not photoreal: collectible art-toy figures in streetwear on a hand-built miniature town in real sunlight. Adult proportions, matte skin, solid sculpted hair, real-fabric clothes with a coarse soft weave. One invented sunny hill town used for every trip: painted houses in cream, terracotta, mint and sky blue, cobbled streets, low walls, plain bunting. No letters, numbers or clocks anywhere. The stadium is only a soft cream bowl with four floodlight masts and plain flags, plus its sound; other fans are still, soft colour shapes holding scarves up. Near every ground stands the bag hut, a small striped hut with shelves of bags. Palette: cream base, teal for Timo, coral for Luna, sunflower yellow shared, deep violet as the darkest colour, no black and no grey. The trip scarf is one half teal and one half coral with a cream fringe and belongs to no club; the home colours of the town are cream and violet. Light: always sun, low and golden, always from screen left and a little in front of the faces. Camera: as if a third friend is filming, at eye level, close. Full-frame 9:16.

## Music theme
"Tick Tock Clap", made for the series: sunny afro-house with an amapiano bounce at exactly 120 beats a minute, built in separate layers. Timo is a tidy tick-tock on the beat. Luna is a lazy log drum with a cowbell that lands a little late. When they agree, both lock under a five-clap stand pattern (clap, clap, clap-clap-clap) and a rough three-note "oh-oh-oh" from three or four young voices. Tick-tock from frame one, tick-tock alone on the "No", the full groove on the hard cut, the voices on the turn, the last three claps on the card. Natural sound is as loud as the music.

## Caption style
Only the spoken line, nothing else. Bold rounded sans-serif, sentence case, cream letters on a soft deep-violet plate. One typeface, one size, one position in every film: centred about two thirds of the way down the frame, above the platform's own text and buttons and clear of the right edge. Two to six words. It appears on the first syllable and stays at least a second and a half. Never two texts at once, no header, no coloured words, no emoji, no pop effects. Start pictures are composed so that no face sits in the caption band.

## The shape of a film
22 to 30 seconds, at most seven shots, then a two-second card and a loop.
1. Frame one: the want and the thing in the way, both visible. No title, no logo.
2. It gets worse, and the cat sees it.
3. The offer and the "No".
4. Hard cut: both are doing it.
5. The turn: the one who refused enjoys it most.
6. The topper: one more picture laugh.
7. The payoff: the first picture turned round, one last short line, hold.

## What never happens
- Anything that must be read in the picture: signs, screens, chats, tickets, shirts with words.
- A header line, a narrator, a to-camera "hey guys", a slogan, an app, a phone, a price, "link in bio".
- A joke that lives only in a line, irony, a mock documentary, a joke that needs another film.
- Humiliation. Nobody loses: not a friend, not a local, not the fan who does not know the clap.
- Romance between Timo and Luna.
- Night, dim rooms, grey colour, middle-aged leads.
- Aggression, flares, rival fans as enemies. Alcohol as the joke. The word "soccer". Real clubs, badges, kits, stadiums, cities, players or brands. Slang of one country.
- More than the two friends plus one local or the cat in a frame. A crowd in focus, match action, the pitch itself (only its light on faces).
- An object passed from hand to hand on camera, precise hand work, mirrors. A hand-over is always a cut.
- A change of outfit, a second look, a patched ending, a post without the platform's AI label.

## End card
Two seconds on a plain warm cream card: the word VENUVOY in deep violet in the middle, the teal-and-coral trip scarf lying flat under it like an underline, and two small words below: "football trips". Sound: the last three claps, the final one ending dry. No logo animation, no app, no link. The card cuts straight back to frame one, so the film loops.

## Posting
The post text carries what the film does not say: "When your friend packs for one night." and "Plan or No Plan: which one are you?". Account line: "Two best friends. Football trips abroad." Never "tag your friend". Every post carries the AI label.
